The revised capital allocations will enable targeted progression on key elements of Government commitments within Level of Ambition 2 objectives.

In relation to the maritime domain, the Commission on the Defence Forces recommended a programme of naval vessel replacement under Level of Ambition 2, to ensure a balanced fleet of a modern ships is reached early in the next decade, this has been accepted in principle by Government.

My Department is preparing a long-term Capability Development Programme which will identify and cost, at a high level, the capability requirements for the Defence Forces out to 2040 across all domains of operation.
I expect to receive in the coming weeks a Regeneration Plan for the Naval Service to address the challenges they faced in recent years from the Chief of Staff of the Defence Forces.

On receipt of the Regeneration Plan and the Capability Development Programme 2028 to 2040, which I intend to bring to Government in the first half of 2026. In finalising these plans I intend to ensure that the Government can make evidence informed decisions on what the balanced fleet of modern ships should be, including decisions regarding the Multi-Role Vessel, and the greater use of technologies. These decisions will also be informed by other relevant information, including the new National Maritime Security Strategy that is expected shortly.

Other projects being progressed include the replacement of secondary armament across the fleet, the provision of 4 motor launches for the Naval Service Reserve, provision for the mid-life upgrade of the four P60 class Offshore Patrol Vessels along with enhanced sub-sea awareness and radar capabilities.

Earlier this year Government announced a new major contract with Thales DMS France for the provision of towed sonar capability. The sonar will be used for monitoring and surveillance in the subsea domain, thus significantly enhancing maritime security. Another project has commenced that aims to provide the Air Corps with the capability to detect, localise, identify, and track sub-surface objects. This capability will be used in conjunction with the new towed sonar capability planned for delivery in 2027, and also with existing Air Corps assets.

Radar capabilities for the Naval Service are being progressed as part of a wider programme of work regarding military radar. A project team comprising senior civil and military personnel has been established to progress three elements to the Military Radar Programme, namely Land based Long Range Primary Radar; Ground Based Air Defence (GBAD) systems, to include a Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems (C-UAS) capability and Maritime (ship-borne) Radar.

In the air domain, capital investment in aircraft continues with the placing of the following contracts in recent years: two new Airbus C-295 in Maritime Patrol Aircraft delivered in 2023; one new Airbus C-295 in a Military Transport configuration delivered in October 2025; one new Dassault Falcon 6X Strategic Reach Aircraft due for delivery today and four Airbus H145M Light Utility Multi-Role Helicopters, with these aircraft in production for phased delivery in 2027 and 2028.

The Air Corps fleet includes eight Pilatus PC-9M aircraft which entered service in 2004. The replacement of these aircraft is being considered as part of the capability development planning process along with the Super-Medium Helicopter Fleet Replacement Project.

question.p: 139. Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Defence to provide an update on Ireland’s air defence capability; if it remains the policy of her Department to pursue the establishment of an Irish Air Force; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72037/25]

speech.p: As Minister for Defence, I am deeply committed to the transformation of the Defence Forces into a modern fit for purpose organisation to defend the State and meet the challenges of today and the future.

In relation to air defence capability, the development of a new ground based air defence system, including Counter Unmanned Aircraft Systems (C-UAS) elements, is a key objective of the overall Military Radar Programme. In line with the Commission on the Defence Forces recommendations, this will be compatible with and integrated into the Recognised Air Picture (RAP). The required air defence capability will need to be deployable, scalable and fully interoperable to protect against any potential air threats.

Good progress is being made across all elements. I was pleased to recently welcome the approval by the Dáil of the Government’s proposal for a substantive capital supplementary estimate of €19 million on the Defence Vote. It is intended that the additional budget allocation will be used to procure, in an accelerated manner, Counter Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS) capabilities for the Defence Forces, that will provide enhanced aerial protection..

It is anticipated that delivery of the C-UAS capability will be available for use by the Defence Forces, if needed, as part of the comprehensive security arrangements to be put in place during Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the European Union in the second half of 2026.

In terms of the policy of my Department to pursue the establishment of an Irish Air Force, the Commission on the Defence Forces recommended in its 2022 report significant changes for the Defence Forces and Defence provision in Ireland. It covers high level Defence Forces structures, defence capabilities, organisation, culture and human resources, the Reserve Defence Force and funding.

In relation to the Air Corps and the Naval Service, the Commission on the Defence Forces stated "Given the importance of service parity, the names of both should change to the Air Force and the Navy respectively." As part of the legislation on Command and Control (C2), it is proposed to change the name of the Air Corps to the Air Force.

The Commission on the Defence Forces also recommended "The Chief of Defence to initiate an immediate force design process assisted by external experts with access to international military expertise, and to include a detailed force design process."

The Defence Forces have established three Force Design teams within the Army, Naval Service and Air Corps and an overarching strategic force design office has also been established to look at the design of a Strategic HQ.

On completion of the force design work by the Defence Forces, the Chief of Staff will submit a report on Force Design to me for review. This is complicated and challenging work which we need to get right to ensure that we design a modern force which is fit for purpose for future generations.

question.p: 140. Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Defence if she will report on her preparations for the security dimensions of the EU presidency. [72049/25]

speech.p: As the Deputy will be aware, preparations for the Presidency are now intensifying across Government. It is important to note that National Security rests primarily with the Department of Justice and An Garda Síochána. The Defence Forces’ role, as always, is to provide support to An Garda Síochána where specific capabilities are required under the Aid to the Civil Power (ATCP) framework.

An Garda Síochána is central to the security planning and preparation. It has established a dedicated European Union Presidency co-ordination office to oversee all aspects of operational planning, logistics and inter-agency engagement.

Support during the Presidency may include security-related and logistical assistance from across the Defence Forces — the Army, Naval Service and Air Corps — in response to requirements identified by An Garda Síochána. The Defence Forces and An Garda Síochána maintain a strong working relationship, and engagement has already taken place in respect of preliminary security planning. Further engagement with colleagues in the Department of Justice and AGS will ensure early visibility of any formal requests for Defence Forces assistance.

question.p: 141. Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Defence the measures being taken by her Department to ensure the protection of critical subsea infrastructure such as the Celtic Interconnector; if she is satisfied that the current operational strength of the Naval Service is sufficient to deter or respond to such threats; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72038/25]

speech.p: The Defence Forces routinely carry out monitoring and surveillance of Ireland’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) using both Naval Service assets and Air Corps maritime patrol aircraft. In addition to at sea monitoring, the Naval Operations Command Centre in Haulbowline carries out remote monitoring twenty four hours a day, seven days a week.

It is clear that protecting critical undersea infrastructure requires collaboration within the State as well as collaboration with other European states to provide a broader understanding of what is occurring in the greater maritime space. This means that Government Departments and agencies, infrastructure operators, the Defence Forces, the private sector and academia all have a part to play. Safeguarding critical undersea infrastructure requires a multifaceted approach with a wide variation of parties involved.

To that end, my Department has taken the lead in the development of a National Maritime Security Strategy following identification of maritime security as a priority in last year’s Defence Policy Review. This strategy is being developed in consultation with national and international stakeholders. I anticipate that this new strategy will provide a roadmap over the next five years to safeguard Ireland’s sovereign maritime interests, ensure safe and secure seas and support international legal order in the maritime domain. I intend to bring this strategy to Government next year.

question.p: 142. Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Defence if she has considered altering height requirements with regard to enlistment eligibility for the Defence Forces. [72039/25]

speech.p: I am informed by the Defence Forces that candidates applying for positions in the Defence Forces are required to meet specific standards for military service, as laid down in Defence Forces Regulations, made pursuant to the Defence Act 1954, as amended and extended. These Regulations provide for a minimum height requirement for enlistment for both male and female candidates of 157.48cm.

The determination of a minimum height standard for enlistment in the Defence Forces is based on the requirement that all members can meet the physical demands of military training and operations thereafter, with service Personal Load Carrying Equipment, whether they are at home or overseas.

While there are no plans at present to alter the height requirements for enlistment, the conditions for entry to and for service in the Defence Forces, including the methodology used for assessments, are subject to continuous review and modification having regard to the needs of the organisation, health and safety and the development of best practices.

question.p: 143. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Defence the position regarding Ireland's preparedness for a significant drone attack on airports or any other significant capital infrastructure; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71463/25]

speech.p: The Government is fully committed to ensuring that the State remains well protected against evolving security challenges, including the misuse of drones. Ireland’s arrangements in this area are grounded in a whole-of-Government approach, led by the competent authorities and supported, where appropriate, by the Defence Forces.

As the Deputy will be aware, primary responsibility for national security rests with An Garda Síochána and the Department of Justice. The Defence Forces, in line with long-standing Government policy, provide specialist support to An Garda Síochána under the Aid to the Civil Power (ATCP) mechanism when specific capabilities are required. This framework allows for a coordinated and proportionate response to drone-related risks, including those posed by malicious actors or disruptive third parties.

I would emphasise that the relevant security agencies continuously assess threats and maintain established arrangements for responding to unauthorised drone activity. These matters are also considered regularly at senior level, including through the National Security Committee.

Strengthening Defence Forces capability is a key priority for this Government. Work is progressing at pace on the Military Radar Programme, which represents the most significant enhancement of our surveillance and airspace awareness capabilities in the history of the State. A dedicated civil-military team is advancing all three elements of the programme: long-range primary radar, ground-based air defence including Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems (C-UAS), and maritime radar. Elements of this capability will begin phased roll-out from 2026, ahead of the timeline for full programme delivery.

In addition, the Office of Emergency Planning within my Department manages the National Risk Assessment on a three-year cycle. In the most recent assessment, the disruptive use of drones was formally identified for the first time as a national-level risk. The Department of Transport is the designated lead for this risk, and my Department will engage closely with them and with other stakeholders to assist in their preparedness.

question.p: 144. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Defence her views on whether much of the Defence Forces housing stock is badly in need of repair; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71651/25]

speech.p: There is currently an extensive programme of investment in accommodation for serving Defence Forces personnel across all military installations. Since the launch of the Infrastructure Development Plan in January 2020, numerous accommodation projects, at a combined cost of approximately €49.7m, have been completed and provided 775 beds.

In terms of the Defence Forces residential housing stock, there are currently three (3) properties which are vacant and require a medium level of refurbishment. A further eighty (80) residential properties are uninhabitable and none of these properties can be brought up to a habitable standard without significant work, and many were built prior to the introduction of building regulations. As such, considerable work is needed to bring them up to modern standards. My officials are engaged with the Defence Forces to have these projects included into the existing infrastructure development plan. It is intended to begin the procurement phase for this refurbishment programme in 2026.

p.i: Question No. 145 answered with Question No. 122.

question.p: 146. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Defence the additional defence funding allocated under the revised National Development Plan that will be provided for Collins Barracks, Cork; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71838/25]

speech.p: As I announced last week, the revised NDP Capital allocation for the Defence Vote Group will provide €1.7 billion in capital funding to Defence out to 2030. This represents an increase of €600 million (55%) on the previous baseline of €1,100 million. For 2026, the Defence capital allocation will increase by €85 million to €300 million. Full details of the Defence NDP 2026-2030 Sectoral Plan are available on the Government website gov.ie.

Capital Investment in Defence primarily provides for the renewal, retention and acquisition of major defence equipment and defence infrastructural development – expenditure which enhances and supports military capabilities and contributes to a more secure and resilient society.

The Defence Forces Infrastructure Development Plan (IDP) currently sets out a programme of infrastructural project delivery to 2027. It reflects the complex environment in which the Defence Forces operate and the corresponding need for appropriate infrastructure to provide for accommodation and training of personnel, as well as the maintenance and storage of equipment.

The IDP is iterative in nature thus ensuring that it remains relevant and that investment is targeted where most needed and aligns with a range of other factors encompassing funding availability, delivery capacity, timing, interdependency with equipment projects and linkage to strategic capability development goals.

Within these overarching IDP structures, the Personnel Support Services Resource Centre, the Infrastructure and Utilities Office and several ablution areas within Collins Barracks Cork have benefitted from recent upgrades. In addition, an accommodation upgrade is also underway in Block 1, Collins Barracks while a refurbishment of the Security Duty Centre and the development of a new Garaging Facility in Collins Barracks are currently at a design stage.

Over the 2026-2030 timeframe, €400 million is being allocated to infrastructural investment on the Defence NDP Sectoral Plan, a level of funding, which will inform and enable associated future IDP processes and deliver enhanced accommodation, offices, gyms etc to military installations throughout the country, together with more targeted investment on the development of specific requirements such as aircraft hangars and naval berthage capacity.

question.p: 147. Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Defence the progress being made to update the Army Pensions Act 1937 following the case of a person (details supplied) who has been refused an Army pension following the death of their son in Lebanon; if interim solutions are being considered for the situation; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71890/25]

speech.p: The Army Pensions Acts 1923-1980 constitutes a military occupational injuries code which operates separately from, but in addition to, the Defence Forces retirement benefit (superannuation) provisions.

The Acts primarily provide for disability pensions, and other allowances and gratuities, and they further allow for the award of a Dependent’s Allowance to the widow, children and other dependants of any member of the Defence Forces killed in the course of duty.

The issue in the specific case you refer to relates to a request to transfer a dependant’s allowance previously awarded to a dependant (now deceased) to their spouse; it is not related to a refusal of an Army pension.

There is no scope under the existing legislation for a transfer or grant of this particular type of allowance to another person on the death of the original recipient of the allowance; it can only be granted to a specified person for their lifetime.

A comprehensive review of the legislative provisions and the relevant circumstances of this case has been carried out. Following on from recently received legal advice, a potential administrative solution has been identified and pending approval of that, my officials will make direct contact with the person in question. My officials will also update the Deputy directly at that point.

Any amendment to the legislation could have potential implications for Defence Forces’ pensions in the first instance, and for pension schemes across the wider public sector. It is important to highlight that any changes to military pension scheme terms and conditions, including for dependant’s benefits, cannot be made by my Department in isolation and would be subject to consultation with, and the approval of, the Minister for Public Expenditure National Development Plan and Reform. On this basis there are no immediate plans to amend the existing Army Pensions legislation.

question.p: 148. Deputy Edward Timmins asked the Minister for Defence the steps being taken to ensure retention of staff in the Defence Forces; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72035/25]

speech.p: I would like to assure the Deputy that attracting and retaining talented individuals and encouraging them to stay and enjoy a fruitful career in the Defence Forces is a priority. Significant work has been undertaken over the past five years to transform the Defence Forces and is having a tangible impact with the stabilisation of overall staffing levels in the Defence Forces.
In addition to a programme of cultural transformation, which is underway, specific actions in retention, which have been delivered, include:
• Significant progress on pay;
• The extension of the existing Service Commitment Scheme for Air Corps pilots, to Air Traffic Control (ATC) personnel;
• An increase in the mandatory retirement age to 62;
• The extension of private healthcare to all ranks in the Defence Forces;
• Provision of fitness, training and sports facilities across its installations;
• Progress on the 2023-2027 Defence Forces Infrastructure Development Plan (IDP) with the highest level of financial resources in the State’s history;
• The provision of excellent training and education opportunities;
• The implementation of the Working Time Directive.
Work is continuing to build on these initiatives through the delivery of a Strategic HR Change Programme, which includes:
• The transformation of Career and Talent Processes and Promotion Systems;
• Remote Learning Solutions;
• A Coaching and Mentoring Programme;
• Flexible Work Practices and Family Friendly Policies.

Local Bargaining has emerged as an important tool to address targeted issues related to workforce retention, particularly within critical skill areas. A range of bespoke proposals are currently under consideration that seek to improve job satisfaction, enable professional development, and address known pinch points affecting career progression and operational continuity.

In January 2025, a Retention Team was set up in the Defence Forces to start building a clear pathway to reduce overall attrition across the Defence Forces. The first focus has been on stabilising the workforce through targeted, evidence-led actions.
Work is well underway on the Defence Forces Retention Strategy, with support from an external partner.

Looking further ahead, the Defence Forces Strategic Workforce Plan is being developed. This plan will set out how the organisation can best balance its workforce in terms of numbers, structure, and skills over the coming years.

question.p: 149. Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Defence the investment planned for enhancing Ireland’s cybers-security capabilities within the Defence Forces; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72014/25]

speech.p: Following the establishment of the Joint Cyber Defence Command (JCDC), a Defence Forces Cyber-Defence Strategy 2024 to 2027 was published last year. This Strategy sets out a comprehensive road map to ensure that the Defence Forces achieve operational capability in this new domain.

To give effect to this Strategy, the assignment of 19 Defence Forces specialist posts has been approved for this unit. This includes the assignment of a Brigadier General to the role. My Department is engaging with the Public Appointments Service to recruit 10 civilian cyber specialists who will be embedded in this new Cyber Unit, it is intended that such posts will be filled as soon as possible. To that end, recruitment campaigns are under way to fill these roles with an initial focus on roles related to cyber threat intelligence and cyber resilience.

I am satisfied that from a Defence perspective we are developing a positive trajectory to ensure that the new Cyber Command Unit is well positioned to meet the ambitious targets set out in the Cyber Strategy.

question.p: 150. Deputy Brian Stanley asked the Minister for Defence the military equipment that has been transferred from the Irish Defence Forces to the Ukraine Armed Forces and government of Ukraine over the duration of the war since the invasion by Russia; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71891/25]

speech.p: While Ireland may be militarily neutral, we are not politically neutral and together with our EU partners, Ireland has been resolute in our response to Russia’s illegal, unjustifiable and morally reprehensible war against Ukraine.

I, and the rest of the Government are committed to working with our European and Ukrainian counterparts to maintain our solidarity with Ukraine and to ensure Ukraine gets the support it needs to defend itself against brutal Russian aggression.

Through our Military Representatives and Officials based in Brussels, my Department is kept informed of Ukraine’s support needs on an ongoing basis and actively explores ways in which Ireland can continue provide non-lethal support, including through the donation of equipment.
To date, the military equipment donated has included :
200 units of body armour delivered in March 2022
2 large de-mining vehicles (DOKING Mine Flails) in February 2023
65 vehicles delivered in June 2024 and September 2025 which included a Fire Truck, ambulances, trucks and minivans.
5 mobile radar defence systems (Giraffes) plus an additional 2 for spare parts delivered in June 2025
3 Demining Robots (Reachers) delivered in September 2025
All equipment donated to date has had no impact on the operational capacity of the Defence Forces and were otherwise exiting from service.
The Defence Forces are continually examining all potential opportunities to donate further equipment and vehicles to the Ukrainian Armed Forces.

p.i: Question No. 151 answered with Question No. 121.

question.p: 152. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Defence the measures being taken to create additional accommodation for military personnel in Collins Barracks, Cork; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71839/25]

speech.p: At present, construction is ongoing for the refurbishment of Block 1 Officer/NCO Accommodation. This project is to provide 25 bedrooms for those personnel based in Collins Barracks in the newly refurbished Block. It is expected to be completed in mid-2026.

The Deputy may also wish to note that the new Accommodation Block for 41 personnel was completed in 2024 increasing the supply of single living-in (SLI) accommodation for enlisted personnel stationed in Collins Barracks

My Department also allocates funding each year to the Defence Forces for the maintenance, repair and upkeep of its building stock. This year a devolved budget of €12.5 million was assigned by my Department to the Defence Forces for these tasks. The individual prioritisation of specific projects to be carried out is solely a matter for the Defence Forces in keeping with the delegated nature of this budget.

question.p: 153. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Defence if she will report on the Defence Force's existing capabilities for detecting, assessing and responding to unauthorised drone activity within the State; and whether current resources, equipment and training are adequate given the increasing prevalence of unmanned aerial systems. [71841/25]

speech.p: The Government is fully committed to ensuring that the State remains well protected against evolving security challenges, including the misuse of drones. Ireland’s arrangements in this area are grounded in a whole-of-Government approach, led by the competent authorities and supported, where appropriate, by the Defence Forces.

As the Deputy will be aware, primary responsibility for national security rests with An Garda Síochána and the Department of Justice. The Defence Forces, in line with long-standing Government policy, provide specialist support to An Garda Síochána under the Aid to the Civil Power (ATCP) mechanism when specific capabilities are required. This framework allows for a coordinated and proportionate response to drone-related risks, including those posed by malicious actors or disruptive third parties.

I would emphasise that the relevant security agencies continuously assess threats and maintain established arrangements for responding to unauthorised drone activity. These matters are also considered regularly at senior level, including through the National Security Committee.

Strengthening Defence Forces capability is a key priority for this Government. Work is progressing at pace on the Military Radar Programme, which represents the most significant enhancement of our surveillance and airspace awareness capabilities in the history of the State. A dedicated civil-military team is advancing all three elements of the programme: long-range primary radar, ground-based air defence including Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems (C-UAS), and maritime radar. Elements of this capability will begin phased roll-out from 2026, ahead of the timeline for full programme delivery.

In addition, the Office of Emergency Planning within my Department manages the National Risk Assessment on a three-year cycle. In the most recent assessment, the disruptive use of drones was formally identified for the first time as a national-level risk. The Department of Transport is the designated lead for this risk, and my Department will engage closely with them and with other stakeholders to assist in their preparedness.

question.p: 154. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Defence the number of naval vessels that can currently be put to sea simultaneously; and the number required under Level of Ambition 2. [71895/25]

speech.p: The Naval Service currently has a fleet of eight vessels. Four of the vessels are regularly deployed on Maritime Defence and Security Operations (MDSO). These four vessels consist of three P60 class vessels as well as the L.É. Aoibhinn (P71) with all four vessels conducting patrols on a rotation basis.

Level of Ambition (LOA) 2 as outlined in the Commission on the Defence Forces (CoDF) Report, includes a recommendation for an accelerated programme of naval vessel replacements, to ensure a balanced fleet of nine modern ships.

p.i: Question No. 155 answered with Question No. 121.

question.p: 156. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Defence her plans to meet with the Defence Forces representative associations; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71655/25]

speech.p: I intend to meet with the Defence Force Representative associations in the New Year. I am very proud to be Minister for Defence and I know that the dedication, duty and patriotism demonstrated by members of our Defence Forces is second to none.

As you know, I launched the Defence Sectoral National Development Plan(NDP) 2026-2030 last week, which is worth €1.7 billion and is the most significant investment package in the Defence Forces in the history of the State. I am determined to ensure that members of our Defence Forces have the equipment, infrastructure and capabilities they need to operate safely and effectively, at home and abroad. The global geopolitical situation is more volatile today than at any time since the end of the Second World War.

I look forward to engaging with the Representative Associations, and getting further insight into the issues of interest to them. I know a lot of progress has been made in recent years on pay and conditions. I am interested to hear the key issues currently affecting their members. I am also interested to hear PDFORRA and RACOs views on the implementation of the Working Time Directive. In short, I am committed to constructive and meaningful engagement with the Associations in the months and years to come. I very much appreciate the work of the Representative Associations on behalf of our personnel in the Defence Forces.

question.p: 157. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Defence if she will provide an update on planned investment in the Defence Forces facilities in Cork, including Collins Barracks; if any upgrades, refurbishments, or expansions are scheduled to support personnel stationed in the Cork region; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71887/25]

speech.p: The Deputy will be pleased to hear that the following projects are currently underway in Cork:
• Haulbowline New Storage Facility for 76mm Gun System
• Haulbowline Block 9 (office) refurbishment
• Haulbowline Modular Accommodaton - (50 beds)
• Fort Davis New Storage Facility
• Collins Barracks Refurbishment of Block 1(accommodation)
• Collins Barracks Refurbishment of Security Duty Centre
The Deputy may also wish to note that the following key infrastructure development projects are in the procurement pipeline and/or design stage :
• Bere island New sewage treatment facility & water main
• Kilworth Waste Water Treatment Plant
• Haulbowline Waste Water Treatment Plant
• Collins Barracks Garaging
• Haulbowline Dredging (of harbour basin)
• Haulbowline Remediation of ISPAT site
• Haulbowline Old Comms Building Fire Repair & Upgrade
• Haulbowline Cadets Mess - internal alterations and refurb
• Haulbowline New Gym at Old Tank Building
• Haulbowline ISPAT Site Development - New Entrance / Security Access
• Haulbowline Additional berthage - West Wall, Graving Dock
• Haulbowline Main Workshops Dockyard
• Haulbowline ISPAT Site Development
• Haulbowline Additional berthage and associated works
• Haulbowline Block 6 – Accommodation.
• Haulbowline Block 10 – Office Accommodation

question.p: 158. Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Taoiseach the protocol for the flying of the national flag; and the proposals, to increase awareness and knowledge of the protocol. [71269/25]

speech.p: It is expected that the National Flag will be treated at all times with appropriate respect by those who use it. Guidelines on the flying of the National Flag are published on gov.ie. These guidelines include comprehensive information on the history and design of the National Flag as well as advice on flying and displaying the National Flag, including appropriate occasions and times for flying the National Flag and the protocol for half-masting and displaying the National Flag during times of mourning. The guidelines also include instructions for folding, hoisting, lowering, and general care and respect for the National Flag.

question.p: 159. Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Taoiseach if his Department, and agencies under the Department’s remit, purchase data on the habits and activities of social media users and other platforms; if so, the reasons for purchasing such data; and the amount spent in 2024 and 2025 year to date on such expenditure, in tabular form. [70873/25]

speech.p: The Department of the Taoiseach does not purchase such data and nor does the National Economic and Social Development Office - the only agency under the Department’s remit.

question.p: 160. Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Taoiseach when his Department will publish a new statement of strategy. [71639/25]

speech.p: The Department of the Taoiseach's Statement of Strategy 2025-2028 was approved by Government on 7th October 2025 and laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas on 10th December 2025. The Statement is published on gov.ie in English at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-the-taoiseach/organisation-information/department-of-taoiseach-statement-of-strategy/ and in Irish at www.gov.ie/ga/roinn-an-taoisigh/eolas-eagraiochta/department-of-taoiseach-statement-of-strategy/.

question.p: 161. Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Taoiseach the amount his Department has spent on translation services from a company (details supplied) for the years 2020 to 2025 to date, in tabular form. [72076/25]

speech.p: The Department of the Taoiseach has not engaged the services of the company in question during the period 2020 to date in 2025.

question.p: 162. Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her engagements regarding the ongoing funding of the peace plus programme as part of the EU MFF post-2027; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71328/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: In advance, and since, the publication of the 2028 – 2034 Multiannual Financial Framework my Department and the Department of Finance have proactively engaged on Ireland’s overarching position on the next long-term EU budget.

As part of this engagement, Ministers and officials have advocated for Ireland’s priorities across a range of key areas, including agriculture, competitiveness, security and external action. Support for the PEACE PLUS programme, including appropriate financing, have been and will continue to be an essential priority for the Government.

It is clear that the practical and demonstrable commitments within the PEACE PLUS programme have had significant benefits to reconciliation and peace on the island of Ireland. We must not take this for granted. The programme also is a clear illustration of the strength and foresight of the Union to secure peaceful outcomes, as well as Europe's collective and continued commitment to long-lasting peace and reconciliation. Inclusion of the Fund in the proposal is therefore very welcome and I, alongside my colleagues, will continue to advocate for its continuation.

While implementation of the PEACE PLUS is under the remit of the Minister for Public Expenditure Infrastructure Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, negotiations on the Multiannual Financial Framework are conducted through the General Affairs Council. This meeting is attended by Minister for European Affairs, Thomas Byrne T.D. In the course of his engagements here, the Minister has advocated extensively for Ireland’s position on the PEACE PLUS programme.

I, alongside my officials and other responsible Ministers and Departments, will continue to engage proactively to ensure the significance of the PEACE PLUS programme to long-lasting peace and reconciliation on the island of Ireland is well understood and reflected in the budget.

question.p: 163. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the position regarding her Department's travel advisory for Irish citizens against travel to Ecuador; the basis for this decision; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71368/25]

164. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the position regarding her Department's travel advisory for Irish citizens against travel to Ecuador; if her attention has been drawn to the fact that the knock on effect means travel to the Galapagos Islands is advised against as a part of Ecuadorian territory; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71369/25]

165. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her attention has been drawn to the contrary position of the UK Government in relation to advisory on travel to the Galapagos Islands; the basis for this difference; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71370/25]

166. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her attention has been drawn to an email sent to her (details supplied); the actions she will take to respond and engage on the substantive issues raised in relation to travel advisories from her Department; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71371/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 163, 164, 165 and 166 together.
I propose to take PQs 71368/25, 71369/25, 71370/25, and 71371/25 together

My Department publishes advice for outward travel in respect of more than 200 countries and territories. The advice provides an objective assessment of the risks Irish citizens could face while travelling, working, or living overseas, with a view to helping them make informed decisions.

The advice is based on consultation with our embassies and consulates on the ground, the relevant local authorities in each country and other partners as appropriate. Our Travel Advice remains under regular review.
While my Department’s travel advice pages set out a security rating associated with travel to specific locations, any decision to travel is the citizen’s responsibility.
The Deputy can find further information on my Department's travel advice and security ratings at this link: www.ireland.ie/en/dfa/overseas-travel/know-before-you-go/security-ratings/.

question.p: 167. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her Department's plans to expand Ireland's diplomatic presence across Australia; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71396/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Australia and Ireland share close and long-standing connections, underpinned by strong people-to-people links. In 2026, we will celebrate 80 years of diplomatic relations with Australia and our Missions are engaged in a range of activities both to mark the anniversary and to deepen bilateral engagement and cooperation at multilateral level.

Ireland is currently represented by two Diplomatic Missions in Australia, with an Embassy in Canberra and a Consulate General in Sydney. In early 2026, that representation will increase to three missions when we open a Consulate General in Melbourne. Plans are well under way for the opening of the Consulate and Marie-Claire Hughes has been appointed as Consul General. This will bring Ireland's diplomatic presence to 18 missions in the Asia Pacific region.

The Embassy and the Consulates work to promote and protect Irish interests in Australia, to strengthen political and economic relationships, to support the Irish community and to promote cultural ties and the Irish arts. In addition, our Honorary Consul in Perth provides consular services and assistance to Irish citizens, supports local Irish community efforts and assists in developing trade and economic relations with Western Australia. Our missions also work closely with the State Agencies to promote trade, tourism and inward investment.

question.p: 168. Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the number of Irish citizens who have sought assistance from the Irish Embassy and Consulates in China in 2023 and to date in 2025, by year, in tabular form. [71415/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has a long and proud track record of providing high quality consular services to Irish citizens abroad. This is a vital public service and a key priority of my Department.

Consular assistance was provided in 53 cases by our Embassy in Beijing, as well as our Consulates General in Shanghai and Hong Kong since 1 January 2023. The numbers of cases recorded, arranged by year and the Embassy or Consulate which provided the assistance, is outlined below.

question.p: 169. Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the consideration given for Ireland to join the International Freedom of Religion or Belief Alliance; and the work that has been undertaken to secure the appointment of a Special Envoy for the Promotion of Freedom of Religion or Belief at the EU. [71637/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion (more commonly referred to as freedom of religion or belief) is regarded as a fundamental freedom, provided for under Article 18 of both the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the International Convention on Civil and Political Rights.
The promotion of freedom of religion or belief is a priority for Ireland’s international human rights engagement.

We advance this freedom both in our multilateral and bilateral engagements. Most recently, at the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in October, Ireland restated our concern for the persecution of people on the basis of their religion. In particular, we condemned all acts of hatred during the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Religion or Belief.

Ireland is a member of the International Contact Group of Freedom of Religion or Belief and the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance. We continue to work within the EU to address the persecution of persons on the basis of their religion or belief. The current EU Action Plan for Human Rights and Democracy 2020 – 2024 (now extended to 2027) includes an express reference to stepping up action to combat discrimination on any ground, including religion or belief.

Ireland is not a member of the International Freedom of Religion or Belief Alliance though this is a matter we keep under active review. However, we are committed members of the related groups to which Ireland already belongs. Ireland has an unwavering and strong commitment to the promotion of freedom of religion or belief.

In regards to the Special Envoy for the Promotion of Freedom of Religion or Belief at the EU, this is a position which is filled by the European Commission. It is our understanding that the position has been without a representative since December 2024. We note that the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, has committed to filling the position and we look forward to working with the new Special Envoy once appointed.

question.p: 170. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her attention has been drawn to the fact that a number of governments , including most recently the government of the Netherlands have moved to accept that autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty is the most feasible solution to the Saharan dispute; if in this regard the Government is reviewing its current position; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71715/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Ireland’s position on Western Sahara has been, and continues to be, guided by the aim of achieving a just and lasting political solution that will provide for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara. Ireland’s engagement on this issue will also continue to take account of the role of, and the insights provided by, the Personal Envoy of the UN Secretary-General for Western Sahara, Staffan de Mistura.
Officials in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade continuously keep any relevant developments under review, including in the context of EU and UN discussions.

On 31 October, the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 2797, extending the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) for one year until 31 October 2026. Ireland is considering the implications of the MINURSO mandate renewal following its adoption.

Officials at the Headquarters of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and in the Mission network continue to be in contact with relevant parties in support of efforts to achieve a solution to this long-standing dispute.

question.p: 171. Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will review the case of a missing Irish person in Gran Canaria (details supplied); and if she will make a statement on the matter. [71721/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I can confirm that officials in my Department, including in the relevant Irish mission, are aware of this case and are providing consular assistance.

As with all consular cases, a dedicated consular officer has been assigned to the family of the Irish citizen who is missing and they remain in contact. The consular officer has provided support and advice to the citizen and their family in accordance with the Department’s Consular Assistance Charter.
I wish to assure the Deputy that officials in my Department will continue to provide all appropriate consular assistance to the citizen.

question.p: 173. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she will report on the 2030 Roadmap on Ukraine-Ireland Partnership that was signed with President Zelenskyy on 2 December 2025. [70939/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: On 2 December, an Taoiseach and President Zelenskyy signed the 2030 Roadmap on Ukraine-Ireland Partnership at Government buildings.

The Roadmap, which represents a key outcome of the visit of President Zelenskyy to Ireland, builds on the bilateral Agreement on Support for Ukraine and Cooperation between Ukraine and Ireland, signed in Kyiv on 4 September 2024.

The Roadmap contains a series of commitments to develop cooperation with Ukraine, which will strengthen bilateral relations across a range of areas, including political and security cooperation; support for Ukraine’s recovery and reconstruction; cooperation in innovation and education; economic cooperation, including the establishment of an annual Ireland Ukraine Economic Forum; and cultural cooperation.

The Roadmap further highlights Ireland’s support for accountability mechanisms in relation to the conflict in Ukraine, and contains reference to our intention to sign the Convention establishing a Claims Commission for Ukraine, which is being established within the framework of the Council of Europe.

The Roadmap includes a commitment by Ireland to provide an additional €100 million in non-lethal military support for Ukraine, building on the figure of €100m in military support already provided in 2025. The Roadmap also contains a contribution of €25 million to support Ukraine’s energy needs.

Other areas include continuing support for Ukraine's EU accession path, including during our EU Presidency in the second half of 2026, and a commitment to share with Ukraine our experience of engagement as an EU Member State.
The Roadmap also establishes an annual Strategic Dialogue between Ireland and Ukraine at the level of Foreign Minister, the first of which was held on 2 December in Dublin.

question.p: 174. Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade his engagements with the government of Burma/Myanmar and its embassy regarding reported election irregularities in the country (details supplied). [72177/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The situation in Myanmar continues to be of grave concern to the Government. We have seen an appalling humanitarian tragedy unfold in that country since the military attempted to seize power in an illegal coup in 2021. Thousands of civilians have been killed, and millions have been displaced or forced into poverty and hunger.

My Department has been closely following developments in Myanmar, including the latest developments surrounding the electoral process announced earlier this year by the so-called State Security and Peace Commission. The European Union issued a strong and comprehensive statement on 10 December - International Human Rights Day - which Ireland fully supports, describing our shared concern regarding the holding of elections in the current context and the serious issues associated with such a move. The essential conditions for free and fair polls are not in place in Myanmar at this time. As the EU statement notes, widespread violence, restrictions on fundamental freedoms, mass detentions, and the exclusion of key political actors severely undermine the credibility of the process.

Ireland implements UN and EU sanctions in relation to Myanmar, which effectively target Myanmar’s military regime, and other groups and entities which threaten democracy, rule of law and peace and security. Ireland is open to consideration of further measures that would be effective in restoring Myanmar’s democratic path and encouraging the cessation of human rights abuses.

Since the coup in February 2021, neither I nor my Department have undertaken actions that would serve to confer the appearance of legitimacy on the military junta. In keeping with that principle, we have not held any bilateral meetings or engagements with the military authorities, or with the Myanmar Embassy in London.

Ireland's Embassy in Bangkok maintains ongoing contact with a range of stakeholders and contacts representing Myanmar civil society, human rights defenders, media and others who are working to support efforts to restore peace, stability and democracy to Myanmar.

My Department will continue to engage both with EU partners and at the UN to urge a return to democracy, stability, and respect for human rights. Ireland supports ASEAN’s efforts to this end, including the full and effective implementation of the ASEAN Five Point Consensus. Ireland joins with our EU partners in urging all stakeholders to prioritise an immediate ceasefire, an end to violence, an inclusive political dialogue, and unhindered humanitarian access.

question.p: 175. Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the progress made over the past 12 months on each of her Department’s Programme for Government commitments, in tabular form; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72192/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Throughout 2025, my Department has made significant progress in delivering on our commitments under the Programme for Government. Updates on relevant commitments are set out in tabular form below. My Department has continued to deliver on behalf of Irish citizens at home and abroad in this time.

In addition to these commitments on which my Department leads, co-leads or plays a significant role, DFAT also contributes to the delivery of a number of other Programme for Government commitments that are led by other Government departments.

td.p: Use the resources of our diplomatic missions and agencies to deliver ambitious targets.

The mission network continues to deliver on all aspects of our high level objectives, guided by the Department's Statement of Strategy, by deepening our global engagement and driving trade and prosperity, responding to the complex global geopolitical context, serving our citizens and communities abroad, and promoting peace and reconciliation on the island of Ireland. The mission network works in close partnership with State agencies as part of Team Ireland overseas.
Support a new US-based Economic Advisory panel which would be made up of senior Irish or Irish-linked decision makers in key business sectors.

The Strategic Economic Advisory Panel (SEAP) was established in Q1 2025. SEAP meetings were held in Washington D.C. in March and in New York in September 2025, attended by the Taoiseach, the Tánaiste and a range of US-based industry leaders, covering a wide range of topics relating to Ireland’s economic relationship with the United States.
Support an open, multilateral, rules-based trade system, promoting free trade policies and economic growth.

Ireland has continued to work closely along with European Union partners to promote free trade policies and in particular to advocate for a strong multilateral trading system with a modernised World Trade Organization at its core. In August, the Government’s Action Plan on Market Diversification was published as a comprehensive approach to promoting Ireland’s trade, tourism, investment and research objectives, and supporting businesses in their market diversification ambitions. The Department also coordinates national engagement at the OECD where Ireland takes a consistent approach in support of an open, multilateral, rules-based trade system, promoting free trade policies and economic growth, including at the OECD. In 2025, the Department also coordinated Ireland’s national engagement at the G20, where Ireland participated as a guest of the South African Presidency in 2025.
Support an ambitious EU trade agenda, promoting new Free Trade Agreements, with proper assurances regarding sustainability, human rights and the protection of our agricultural sector.

Ireland has continued to support an ambitious EU trade agenda, with progress across several negotiations including with Indonesia and India. Ireland has also supported EU engagement with the US as we work towards a new mutually beneficial trade and investment relationship. Throughout, Ireland has consistently emphasised the need for strong sustainability and human rights provisions, and has worked to ensure that agricultural sensitivities are protected. Ireland was active in seeking to secure agreement between the Council and the European Parliament on revising the EU GSP Regulation which is an important tool for providing non-reciprocal, preferential access to the EU for developing and least developed countries. Political agreement was reached on 1 December.

The Arbitration (Amendment) Bill 2025 has passed Second Stage in the Dáil. The Bill, once passed, will enable ratification of the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) and other international agreements containing similar investment dispute resolution provisions, including those with Chile, Mexico, Singapore and Vietnam
Work with like-minded EU countries to stand up for Irish farmers and defend our interests in opposing the current Mercosur trade deal.

The Government has continued to engage at EU level – with both the European Commission and with counterparts in like-minded EU Member States – to voice our concerns with the EU-Mercosur agreement and to interrogate the outcome of negotiations to assess if our concerns have been adequately addressed.
Ensure there is continued support for climate finance delivered through Ireland’s Overseas Development Aid programme, particularly in areas where communities are vulnerable to climate impacts.

At COP26, held in Glasgow in November 2021, the Taoiseach announced that Ireland would provide at least €225 million in climate finance per year to developing countries by 2025. By the end of 2025, we will reach this target. Climate Finance reports are published in arrears. In March 2025, the 2023 Climate Finance Report was launched and highlighted that Ireland provided €159.2 million in international climate finance.
Actively support climate initiatives to address the severe effects of drought, famine, and lack of clean water in collaboration with international partners.

During 2025 Ireland’s climate programming continued to focus on supporting countries and communities most seriously in need, including countries impacted by drought, famine and lack of access to water. For example, in 2025 Ireland provided €5.5 million to the United Nations Central Emergency Relief Fund Climate Action Account which is mandated to respond to climate induced emergencies, €2.5 million to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Global Climate Resilience Platform and €1.5 million to Start Ready. These are emergency response pooled mechanisms for climate induced disasters. Additionally, Ireland continued its partnership with Concern Worldwide, providing €5 million for activities dedicated to addressing acute malnutrition (wasting) in children in the vulnerable drought-prone border regions of Somalia, Ethiopia and Kenya.
Actively advocate for the rights of LGBTQI+ individuals both in Ireland and internationally.

The promotion and protection of the rights of LGBTQI+ persons is a domestic and foreign policy priority for Ireland. Ireland participates in the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia (IDAHOT) and annual Pride events. Ireland is a member of the Equal Rights Coalition, and meets with the group regularly to continue to work on the promotion and protection of the human rights of LGBTQI+ persons globally, while countering the current pushback on LGBTQI+ rights.

Engage in discussions at key international forums, including the EU and the UN, to uphold the universal nature of human rights, ensuring that these rights apply equally to all individuals, regardless of gender identity, sexual orientation, or any other characteristic.
Ireland strongly supports efforts in international human rights fora to promote the rights of LGBTQI+ persons, including at the UN Human Rights Council and the UN General Assembly.

Ireland strongly supported the renewal of the mandate of the UN Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity (SOGI) at the 59th session of the Human Rights Council in July. Ireland also delivered a national statement at the 59th Session of the Human Rights Council, at the Interactive Dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on SOGI, and a statement at the Third Committee of the 80th Session of the UN General Assembly, at the Interactive Dialogue with the Independent Expert on Discrimination based on SOGI. Ireland is also a member of the Group of Friends of the mandate of the Independent Expert on SOGI.

This year at the UN Human Rights Council’s Universal Periodic Review, Ireland raised the rights on LGBTQI+ persons in the recommendations made to: Jamaica, Liberia, Libya, Malawi, Mongolia, Panama, Armenia, Grenada, Guyana, Kiribati, Türkiye and Bosnia Herzegovina.
The promotion and protection of the rights of LGBTQI+ persons is also a priority in Ireland’s campaign for membership of the Human Rights Council, launched in September in New York by the Tánaiste.
Give effect to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance ‘Working Definition of Antisemitism’ and implement the EU declaration on ‘Fostering Jewish Life in Europe’.

Senior members of the Government meet regularly with representatives of Ireland’s Jewish communities, including the Taoiseach, the Tánaiste, the Minister for Justice, and the Minister of State for European Affairs. Most recently, the Tánaiste met with representatives of Ireland’s Jewish community in September. DFAT officials also maintain regular contact with the Jewish community.
Ireland provides an annual grant towards the upkeep of the Auschwitz memorial. This year we provided €50,000 recognizing the importance of the 80th anniversary event.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has worked with JACI (Jewish Arts and Culture Ireland) to develop an exhibition on the links between Lithuania and Ireland’s Jewish Community.
This year, Ireland continued the Crocus project, where young children plant yellow crocus bulbs in October, which bloom in January in remembrance of the victims.
Support artists to access international opportunities through increased funding for Culture Ireland and support for our embassies to promote more bilateral exchanges.
There has been an expansion of specialist cultural attaché programme with new appointments in India, China and South East Asia.

Promote an all-island approach to hosting major international sporting events, building on the Major International Events policy, including supporting the hosting of the 2027 Ryder Cup, Euro 2028, the T20 Cricket World Cup 2030, the Open Championships and bidding for major competitions.

The continuation of a structured and strategic approach to securing the hosting of major sporting events that can deliver all-island benefits, including co-hosting opportunities, is being considered as part of the International Sport Diplomacy Strategy currently under development. This will be informed by the Major International Sports Events Policy and Strategy Framework 2024. Work is also ongoing to establish a formal structure across Government for the coordination of major sporting events.
Maintain and continue to grow the Global Ireland Media Challenge Fund to build capacity of Irish media outlets to undertake quality reporting on international geopolitical events.

The latest application window for the Global Ireland Media Challenge Fund was opened in January 2025, following which six additional media organisations were awarded funding for the 2025-2026 period. Match funding of 52% was achieved and participating organisations have undertaken to create over 2,000 original content pieces under video, print and social media over the 18 month term.
Support the development of the Savings and Investment Union, seeking opportunities to improve competition in key financial sectors and to support the green and digital transitions.
We are actively involved in progressing associated EU legislative measures for a Savings and Investment Union.

Ireland proactively and collaboratively engaged in the negotiations for an EU-wide 2040 climate target. We agreed to a highly ambitious target to reduce emissions by 90% by 2040, based on 1990 levels, while securing stronger language on food security, forestry and land use, renewable energy, and a just transition – including energy affordability. For digital, Ireland strongly supports the ambitious digital simplification package and we are developing a strong, coherent and stable digital regulatory framework. Ireland is making efforts towards increasing resilience and decreasing dependencies in critical digital value chains in an open manner, which means maintaining access to open markets, interoperability, and international collaboration.
Support and implement the European Green Deal, unlocking more of Europe’s renewable energy potential through enhanced EU co-operation and improved European grid connectivity.

Ireland is accelerating the green energy transition by advancing policies which enhance affordability for businesses and households while enabling faster adoption of renewables and robust energy security.

Ireland is also prioritising an EU-wide approach to deployment and investment in grid infrastructure in order to enhance our competitiveness and has engaged proactively with the Commission in the lead up to its publication of the European Grids Package on 16 December 2025.
Projects such as the Celtic Interconnector between Ireland and France, which will be a key first step towards expanding and diversifying interconnections, are also progressing.
Ensure there is an ambitious new European Budget settlement, protecting existing EU programmes and taking action on strategic priorities.

The proposal for the 2028 – 2034 Multiannual Financial Framework was published in July and September this year. Since then, DFAT and the Department of Finance, as co-leads on Ireland’s position, have coordinated across Government to ensure Irish priorities and ambitions are well communicated and advanced. Negotiations are ongoing, and Ireland’s EU Presidency, will come at a critical juncture in this process.
Prioritise economic competitiveness in the EU and continue to promote international trade, as it is vital to the Irish economy.

We are working to implement the files of the Competitive Compass outlined by the Commission. Ireland has also worked to take forward the implementation of the EU Single Market Strategy and is calling for the early publication of the Single Market Roadmap to 2028 with concrete targets and timelines. Moreover, we are opposing the application of a “European Preference” across our industrial policy toolkit. We are prioritising an open economy with free and fair competition and the deepening of the Single Market, which should remain the EU’s main approach to enhancing competitiveness. We are also advocating for Strengthening EU-US cooperation and are expressing caution regarding approaches that could disrupt transatlantic investment flows or global value chains.

Work to strengthen the application and monitoring of the rule of law across the EU, ensuring the non-partisan application of the Rule of Law mechanism, and ensure that all citizens in all member states feel equally protected from those who threaten our values, including their own governments.

Ireland continues to be a strong advocate for the Rule of Law within the EU. We recognise the importance of having the necessary tools to monitor developments across EU Member States and to respond to challenges where they arise. We are therefore supporting efforts led by Commissioner McGrath to strengthen mechanisms to ensure respect for the rule of law in all EU Member States. DFAT worked closely with the Attorney General in preparing Ireland’s national intervention in support of the European Commission’s infringement case against Hungary’s National Sovereignty Protection Law. Through DFAT’s European Enlargement and Fundamental Values Fund (EEFV), Ireland is also providing financial assistance to civil society groups and other bodies in EU Member States where the rule of law is under pressure.
Support sanctions against countries seeking to undermine European democracy.
Ireland implements EU and UN sanctions; this commitment is in progress.
Reduce where possible the regulatory burden simplifying EU rules for the SME and Farming sectors.

The Department has coordinated work across Government on the EU’s simplification agenda to help reduce the regulatory burden, notably for SMEs and farming communities. We have worked with EU partners to make progress on the implementation of the eight Omnibus simplification packages proposed by the Commission so far, which the Commission estimates will lead to administrative savings across the EU of €11 billion per year.

Deliver on plans to increase the number of Irish people applying for positions in the institutions of the European Union, including a communications campaign targeted at school leavers and graduates highlighting the opportunities available, and a partnership with third level providers to do the same.

The Department continues implementing the “A Career for EU strategy” to increase Irish representation in EU institutions. In 2025, physical outreach at second and third-level careers fairs promoted EU careers to school leavers and graduates, while targeted social media campaigns encouraged professional applicants. Minister of State for European Affairs and Defence, Thomas Byrne, TD, addressed students at Higher Options and participated in local radio interviews. The dedicated website ireland.ie/en/eu-jobs received thousands of visits. Extensive training and supports continue for Irish candidates.
Uphold the Irish language’s full status as an official language of the European Union.

The Government is resolute in upholding the Irish language's full and secure status within the EU. Irish is a full official and working language of the Union, and there is no question of its status being diminished. This position is guaranteed by the Treaties and the subsequent Council Regulation No. 2021/168. Since 1 January 2022, Irish has enjoyed complete parity with the EU’s other 23 official languages. This means that all key EU legislative acts and documents are translated into Irish, and citizens have the right to correspond with the EU institutions in Irish. Ireland remains committed to promoting and strengthening the Irish language across the European institutions, recognising its deep cultural and national significance, and its firm foundation as a Treaty language of the Union.
Develop and promote projects which build links and understanding with other EU capitals and regions in the fields of culture, education, research and innovation.

In 2025, Ireland actively promoted Irish culture across EU Member States through a €250,000 fund disbursed through the Mission network in the EU. This funding is specifically allocated to Irish Embassies and Consulates throughout the region to support and facilitate cultural and educational initiatives that showcase Irish heritage, arts and identity. The funding enables Missions to develop and implement targeted cultural programmes that resonate with local audiences across different EU MS.
Stand by the EU’s accession promises, promoting a positive enlargement strategy for Ukraine, the Western Balkans, Moldova and Georgia.

Ireland has continued to promote and support progressing EU Enlargement policy and individual candidacies on a merit-basis. EU Enlargement will be a key priority of our upcoming EU Presidency and Ireland will seek to advance the candidacies of all candidate and potential candidate countries where conditions have been met. In advance of our EU Presidency, in September 2025, Ireland opened embassies in three candidate countries, in Bosnia Herzegovina, Moldova and Serbia. The Minister of State for European Affairs has also visited Albania, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Ukraine throughout 2025 and reaffirmed Ireland’s strong support for their respective EU accession paths. Ireland has also supported several projects to support candidate and potential candidate countries’ EU accession processes, some of which are outlined below.
Promote closer co-operation with candidate countries, assisting these nations to align with EU standards.

A three year 'Ireland for EU Enlargement Programme', funded through EU and Trade Divisions' EU Enlargement and Fundamental Values fund, is being delivered by the Institute of Public Administration (IPA) together with the Podgorica-based Western Balkans Regional School of Public Administration (ReSPA) to support capacity building in candidate countries focusing on the Rule of Law, digitalisation and economic transformations. In November, 48 senior officials from candidate countries travelled to Dublin for further classes and engagements to build capacity and awareness of EU standards and policies.

Ireland has also made a contribution of €1.5 million towards the “Ukraine2EU”, a programme supporting Ukraine’s EU accession path and which is being implemented by Lithuania’s Central Project Management Agency.

Introduce a new John Hume Fund in honour of one of Ireland’s greatest ever patriots and only member of the European Parliament to win a Nobel Prize. This is to be awarded annually by that Parliament to a person or organisation who promotes reconciliation and shared prosperity in Europe.

EU and Trade Policy Division within DFAT has established a new European Parliament Unit this year. The purpose of this unit is to maximise opportunities for effective Irish engagement with the European Parliament, both as a key partner in our ongoing work and in particular with a view to an effective Irish Presidency in 2026. As part of this work, the unit has engaged in initial outreach around the establishment of a John Hume Fund, conducting research on existing awards granted by the European Parliament and gathering views from relevant interlocutors, with a view to recommending a way forward on the establishment of a new fund.
Publish plans for our upcoming Presidency to deliver against strategic priorities for Europe and Ireland.
Work is ongoing to develop Ireland's Presidency priorities and policy programme. In line with convention, Ireland's policy programme for the Presidency will be finalised and published in June 2026

Host an informal meeting of the European Council and a meeting of the European Political Community in Ireland during the Presidency, as well as a programme of between 16 and 20 informal Council meetings at Ministerial level.

Extensive planning work has continued to prepare for the programme of meetings to be hosted across Ireland during our EU Presidency. These will include a summit of the European Political Community, an informal meeting of the European Council and 22 informal Ministerial meetings. Overall, we expect to host more than 250 Presidency events here. DFAT has chaired monthly Inter-Departmental meetings on Operational Presidency Planning to support delivery of the Presidency meeting programme in Ireland.
Seek to bring some of the high-level meetings of our Presidency to cities and counties across Ireland, ensuring the entire country benefits from the profile the Presidency brings.
Planning is underway for six informal Ministerial meetings, as well a range of other conferences, official-level meetings and other events, to take place in regional locations.
Provide for a sustainability policy for the Presidency.
A sustainability policy for Ireland’s EU Presidency in 2026 is in final development and will be launched in Q1 2026.

Continue to work with partners in the region to advocate for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza, the return of all hostages and a surge of humanitarian aid. We will also work with partners to help rebuild Gaza as soon as practicable.

Ireland has welcomed the ceasefire and the agreement on the first phase of the Comprehensive Plan to end the war in Gaza. This is an important first step on a road to peace. Ireland continues to call for humanitarian aid to be directed throughout the entire Gaza Strip at scale.

Ireland has provided 177 tonnes of supplies including tents, blankets, water cans and other vital household items to Gaza under Ireland’s Rapid Response Initiative. 10 trucks of carrying food, supported by Irish Aid in partnership with Plan Ireland, arrived in Gaza in recent weeks for distribution to people who urgently need it. Ireland will also provide an additional €6 million in humanitarian aid for people in Gaza as UN and humanitarian agencies prepare to ramp up aid supplies following the ceasefire. This new contribution brings Ireland’s support for the people of Palestine since October 2023 to more than €102 million, and support in 2025 to over €36 million.

Seek to grow the international coalition of countries supporting a two-state solution through recognition of the State of Palestine and continue to advocate for internationally sponsored political negotiations on achieving a peaceful and secure Israel and Palestine.

Ireland stands ready to play our part in working towards a sustainable peace between Israel and Palestine through the implementation of the two-State solution. Ireland was active in preparing the UN High-level Conference on the Two-State Solution held in New York from 28 - 30 July. The outcome document from the meeting – the New York Declaration – has been endorsed by 142 countries. The Taoiseach attended the re-convened Conference during UN High Level Week in late September. We welcome that the actions in the New York Declaration have influenced the drafting of the US Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict. Ireland is an active member of the Global Alliance for the Implementation of the Two-State Solution and will host a meeting of the Global Alliance in Ireland in late January, where we will share elements of our own experience of a successful peace process in Northern Ireland.
Continue to seek the application of International Law and justice to all sides in the current conflict through the international court system.

Ireland has continued to seek the application of International Law and justice to all sides in the current conflict through the international court system by participation in relevant International Court of Justice proceedings, and support to the International Criminal Court.

Advocate for a meaningful interpretation of Israel’s human rights obligations under the EU-Israel association agreement at European Commission level and continue to advocate a review of the EU Trade Agreement.

Ireland has consistently called for the EU to take concrete action in response to egregious Israeli breaches of human rights and democratic principles. Ireland welcomes proposals from the European Commission to suspend the core trade-related provisions of the EU-Israel Association Agreement. The proposals are a significant step forward. Ireland has made clear our view that the EU must keep the package of measures proposed in response to Israeli human rights and other breaches on the table. In her State of the Union address, the President of the European Commission was clear on the rationale for tabling the package of proposals, which remain valid.
Progress legislation prohibiting goods from Occupied Palestinian Territories following the July 2024 International Court of Justice Advisory Opinion.

In June 2025, the Government approved the General Scheme of the Israeli Settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (Prohibition of Importation of Goods) Bill. The main purpose of the Bill is to prohibit the importation of goods into the State from Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem, in line with the Programme for Government commitment to progress that legislation.
