The next steps in the process, including the timeline for the progress of the Bill, are being considered.
Continue to oppose and condemn Hamas and other groups which bring terror and destruction to their own people and others.
Ireland has consistently condemned Hamas and stated that the PA is the only credible and legitimate interlocutor on the Palestinian side and must be fully engaged.

question.p: 176. Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she plans to expand the Ireland house model in South Africa. [72223/25]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: Since the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1993, Ireland has developed close economic, political and people-to-people ties with South Africa. This was reflected in South Africa’s decision to invite Ireland to participate this year as a guest country in the G20 during the South African G20 Presidency. This year, in October, we also welcomed the successful official visit to Ireland by President Cyril Ramaphosa.

Ireland and South Africa enjoy strong trade and investment flows in both directions. Our Embassy and the state agencies work very closely together on the ground to promote Irish business interests. This includes local market team collaboration and mutual support to ensure successful trade and investment missions to South Africa.

In countries where state agencies have an office, and are situated in the same city as an Embassy or Consulate, our preference is to consolidate the Ireland House model, whereby missions and state agencies are co-located. Accommodating the representatives of the state under one roof improves services to citizens and business and offers opportunities for enhanced value for money.

Given business needs in South Africa, the Enterprise Ireland office is located in Cape Town and the IDA and Bord Bia share a representative who is based in Johannesburg. Embassies are always located in the capital of the country to which they are accredited, so physical co-location with state agencies is not always possible, as in the case of South Africa, where the Embassy is in Pretoria. However, I am pleased that the strong Team Ireland coordination and supports in place ensure that our economic interests are protected and advanced.

question.p: 177. Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if an application (details supplied) has been received; and if she will instruct her Department to assist the family in question. [72301/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: The subject of this Parliamentary Question is not a matter for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

It is not within the responsibility of the Minister to facilitate the humanitarian evacuation of non-Irish citizens to a third country, in this case, to the United States. This would be a matter for the US authorities and queries from the family in question should be directed to the relevant US authorities.

question.p: 178. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if she has spoken formally with the US Ambassador to Ireland since her appointment as Minister; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72400/25]

speech.from: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade
speech.p: I have not yet had the opportunity to speak to the US Ambassador since taking up duty as Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade. I look forward to doing so in the near future.
My predecessor as Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade, Tánaiste Simon Harris T.D., had the opportunity to speak with and meet Ambassador Walsh on a number of occasions.

Developing Ireland's rich political, economic, cultural, and people-to-people links with the United States is a priority for me, just as it is for this Government. I look forward to discussing that with the Ambassador, and to launching a new strategy for Ireland's relationship with the United States in the new year.

question.p: 179. Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to respond to reports of Government plans for six-month lockdowns if subsea cables are hit; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72290/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The National Risk Assessment (NRA) 2023, prepared by the Minster for Defence in conjunction with the Office of Emergency Planning, specifically highlighted an elevated risk to energy infrastructure and singled out an attack on gas interconnectors between Ireland and the UK as a worst-case scenario. This assessment was influenced by incidents elsewhere at that time. My Department has responsibility for this risk and must ensure that mitigations are in place to reduce risk and highlight the need to protect the system against its occurrence.

On 3 December 2024, Exercise Cathal took place in the National Emergency Coordination Centre (NECC). The table-top exercise was led by my Department and tested the whole of government response to a prolonged gas outage in Ireland as a result of the two gas interconnectors being compromised.

While the implications of such a scenario are very significant, and it is likely that repair could take in the order of four to six months, weather dependent, a "six month lockdown" as referenced by the Deputy is not part of the response plans.
The learnings and next steps from the Exercise were presented to the Government Task Force (GTF) on Emergency Planning on 11 March 2025.

Since Exercise Cathal, the Government has progressed the establishment of a Strategic Emergency Gas Reserve which will act as a key mitigation against this risk. Protection of critical infrastructure, including subsea cables and pipelines, falls within the area of national security and as such it would be inappropriate to provide any further detail in that regard.

The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) oversees the overarching emergency plans and works in conjunction with my Department in this regard. ESB Networks, EirGrid and Gas Networks Ireland have robust procedures in place, such as the Natural Gas Emergency Plan (NGEP), which is publicly available. These agencies regularly participate in simulation exercises to test a range of potential scenarios.

question.p: 180. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment in relation to comments that energy companies were price gouging (details supplied), what measures he is taking to prevent energy companies from price gouging and to protect households from this; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72370/25]

202. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he is aware of comments by the Taoiseach that energy companies were price gouging; if he agrees with these comments; the measures he is taking to prevent energy companies from price gouging and to protect households from this; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72369/25]

203. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he is aware of the comments at the Joint Oireachtas Committee Climate, Energy and Environment on 10 December 2025 that price gouging cannot be ruled out; the measures he will take to address this; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72374/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 180, 202 and 203 together.

The electricity and gas retail markets in Ireland operate within an EU regulatory regime wherein these markets are commercial and liberalised. The Commissions for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) ended its regulation of retail prices in the electricity market in 2011, and in the gas market in 2014. Price setting by electricity suppliers is therefore a commercial matter for the companies concerned. Retail prices are influenced by several factors, including wholesale energy prices, system operation costs and supplier hedging. Regarding hedging, suppliers in Ireland were shown to have taken a prudent approach to hedging which had the benefit of protecting final customers from the worst effects of the wholesale price crisis. Conversely, hedging limits the ability of suppliers to reduce prices immediately in line with wholesale price shifts.

The IEA has observed that Irish retail prices have not adjusted at a comparable pace to the decline in wholesale prices, with the energy component of retail prices remaining up to three times that of wholesale prices. While the CRU has found no evidence of market failure or windfall profits in the retail sector in its market monitoring role, the IEA findings underline the importance of progressing the Programme for Government commitment to “commission an independent review into the speed and level of passthrough from wholesale prices to retail prices,”.

I have written to CRU to request that they commence this independent review, building on the work of previous CRU investigations by reviewing the competitiveness of Irish retail energy markets, examining supplier costs, including hedging and pricing practices, and providing comparative price analysis with other EU Member States. It will also assess whether measures are warranted to enhance market responsiveness to wholesale price changes, and make recommendations to ensure that the benefits of lower wholesale prices are felt by consumers. This report will inform the work of the National Energy Affordability Taskforce.

In addition, my Department, is transposing the new Electricity Market Design Directive 2024. This Directive requires regulators to ensure that suppliers implement appropriate hedging strategies to reduce the risk of supply failure.

question.p: 181. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will review the policy whereby the SEAI offers grants for heat pump systems to homeowners whose homes were built and occupied before 2021, with the condition that the grant is available for first-time installations only; if he will include homeowners who initially installed a heat pump system, and are not eligible for grant aid for replacement systems; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72681/25]

197. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will provide grants to replace renewable energy heating systems that have reached the end of their lifespan (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72184/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 181 and 197 together.

My Department funds a number of grant schemes, administered by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), to support homeowners improve the energy efficiency of their buildings, and to promote the adoption of renewable energy systems. These schemes have terms and conditions in place to ensure the transparent administration of public monies.

It is important to note that the grants available through the SEAI aim to maximise emissions reductions and deliver energy savings for the widest range of homeowners possible. The grants which are available, and their respective eligibility criteria, were designed to deliver significant energy savings to homeowners at the best value for money for the Exchequer. Since the funds that are available for energy efficiency are limited, my Department must prioritise their use where they will have the most impact.

Therefore, regarding support for the installation of a heat pump, grants will only be paid in relation to homes where solid fuel, oil/gas boiler or electrical heating (other than a heat pump) is present, or where there is no heating in situ. There is currently no plan to amend these criteria.

My Department, in partnership with the SEAI, continues to ensure that grant schemes terms and conditions, eligibility criteria, and rates are kept under review, taking account of demand, research, innovation, evolving technology and other relevant factors.

question.p: 182. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the number of heat pumps installed since 2020 under the National Retrofitting Programme; the projected installation rate to 2030; and whether his Department has assessed alternative solutions for the 300,000+ rural homes unlikely to be retrofitted. [71512/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Climate Action Plan (CAP) sets out policies, measures and actions to achieve sectoral emissions ceilings for the residential sector.

The National Heat Study, published by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), contains detailed analysis that is being used by my Department to inform the development of policies and measures to decarbonise Ireland’s heating by 2050. The study considered a number of potential decarbonisation options for a wide range of dwellings and business premises. The recommendation of the heat study is that heat pumps are the optimal decarbonisation path for heating systems in buildings, with district heating also being an option that can be widely deployed.

Since 2019, there has been a record level of over €1.6 billion invested in SEAI schemes to support almost 240,000 home energy upgrades, including over 81,000 BER B2s, 18,000 heat pump installations and over 32,000 fully-funded upgrades for households at risk of energy poverty under the Warmer Homes Scheme. In addition, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage funded a further 14,300 Local Authority upgrades, including over 7,250 heat pumps between 2019 to 2024. This means that over 25,000 heat pumps have been installed with Government support since 2019.

The Programme for Government 2025 commits to targeting older homes still using oil to switch to renewable heating systems and to consider the use of sustainable biofuels to reduce emissions from existing home boilers where deep retrofits are not possible in the short term. These commitments are framing the work underway to develop a Heat Policy Statement and the Roadmap to Phase Out Fossil Fuel Heating Systems which will jointly set out Ireland's overarching approach to decarbonising the heat sector.

Increasing the uptake of energy efficiency measures among homeowners continues to be a key priority for my Department working in partnership with the SEAI. Further policies and measures will be introduced on an annual basis to support the achievement of our retrofit and heat pump targets.

question.p: 183. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will publish an analysis comparing the emissions savings from a 20% biofuel blend in existing boilers versus deep retrofitting and heat pump installation. [71513/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The National Heat Study, published by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland, considered a number of potential decarbonisation options for a wide range of dwellings and business premises. These included the use of liquid biofuels, as well as heat pumps and district heating networks. While the recommendation of the Heat Study is that heat pumps are the optimal decarbonisation path for heating systems, the heat study also recognised the potential role for sustainable bioenergy for buildings that require alternative routes to decarbonisation. This is being considered as part of a suite of measures to decarbonise heat.

The Programme for Government 2025 commits to targeting older homes still using oil to switch to renewable heating systems and to consider the use of sustainable biofuels to reduce emissions from existing home boilers where deep retrofits are not possible in the short term. These commitments are framing the work underway to finalise a Heat Policy Statement and prepare a Roadmap to Phase Out Fossil Fuel heating systems, which will jointly set out Ireland's overarching approach to decarbonising the heat sector.

My Department is also working on the introduction of the Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO). Under current proposals, the RHO will obligate suppliers of all fossil fuels used for heating purposes to ensure a proportion of the energy they supply is renewable. As such, all renewable fuels, including bioliquids used for heat that satisfy the sustainability criteria of the Renewable Energy Directive, will be considered eligible for certification under the scheme. Introduction of the RHO is a key objective for me, as Minister, with priority drafting of the Renewable Heat Obligation Bill 2025 now underway.

As part of the RHO development and design process, my Department completed two phases of analysis which included a full impact assessment on the scheme structure, considering critical factors, including the availability of renewable fuels to meet the obligation, the likely economic and social impact of the obligation, and resulting costs to end consumers. Detail in relation to each phase of analysis, including the full assessment carried out on potential obligation rates, is available on gov.ie at:
www.gov.ie/en/department-of-climate-energy-and-the-environment/publications/renewable-heat-obligation/#general-scheme-design

question.p: 184. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the progress on the Programme for Government commitment to consider the use of sustainable biofuels to reduce emissions from existing home boilers where deep retrofits are not possible, including timelines for implementation. [71514/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) is a bioliquid which can be used as a renewable energy source and which, in a transport context, is classified as a biofuel. HVO is currently available for consumers to purchase for use for both transport and heating. The Climate Action Plan includes a range of measures to address the use of fossil fuels in heating systems in buildings, with the National Heat Study, published by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland, containing the detailed analysis that is informing the development of options to decarbonise the heating and cooling sectors in the period to 2050.

The Heat Study considered a number of potential decarbonisation options for a wide range of dwellings and business premises. These included the use of liquid biofuels such as HVO, solid biomass, biogases, as well as heat pumps and district heating networks. The recommendation of the Heat Study is that heat pumps are the optimal decarbonisation path for heating systems, with district heating also being an option that can be widely deployed. However, the Heat Study also recognised the potential role for sustainable bioenergy for buildings that require alternative routes to decarbonisation, and that is being considered as part of a suite of measures to decarbonise heat.

The Programme for Government 2025 commits to targeting older homes still using oil to switch to renewable heating systems and to consider the use of sustainable biofuels to reduce emissions from existing home boilers where deep retrofits are not possible in the short term. These commitments are framing the work underway to finalise a Heat Policy Statement and prepare a Roadmap to Phase Out Fossil Fuel heating systems, which will jointly set out Ireland's overarching approach to decarbonising the heat sector.

My Department is working on the introduction of a Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO) for the heat sector. Under current proposals, the RHO will obligate suppliers of all fossil fuels used for heating purposes to ensure a proportion of the energy they supply is renewable. As such, all renewable fuels, including bioliquids used for heat that satisfy the sustainability criteria of the Renewable Energy Directive, will be considered eligible for certification under the scheme. The RHO Heads of Bill were approved by Government and drafting of the RHO legislation is currently underway.

question.p: 185. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the rationale for setting initial Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO) rates at 1.5% and 3%, given Departmental analysis indicating that achieving RES-H targets requires at least 15% by 2030; and whether he will revise these rates upward for liquid fuels. [71515/25]

186. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will consider a phased trajectory for liquid fuels under the Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO), starting at 5% and rising to 15% by 2030, as proposed by industry stakeholders' if he will publish his Department’s cost and emissions modelling for this approach. [71516/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 185 and 186 together.

Introduction of the Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO) is a key priority for me, as Minister, with the primary objective of supporting the achievement of Ireland's renewable heating targets by the most cost-effective means available.

Design of the RHO has included two phases of analysis, stakeholder engagement activities, and extensive industry engagement. Feedback received informed a full impact assessment on the scheme structure, considering critical factors, including the availability of renewable fuels to meet the obligation, and the likely economic and social impact of the obligation. Results of this work informed the general scheme of the Renewable Heat Obligation Bill 2025, recently approved by Government.

Decisions made in relation to initial starting rates were based on an extensive examination of the scale of obligation required to meet Ireland’s renewable heat targets, and resulting impact on end consumer costs. While no final decisions have been taken in relation to the next RHO rate increase in year 3, or a final RHO target level, more ambitious rates have been examined that would enable us to meet our renewable energy and climate targets.

summary.i: Question No. 186 answered with Question No. 185.

question.p: 187. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to publish an assessment of the consumer cost impact of introducing a 5% biofuel blend for home heating; and whether his Department will review excise and carbon tax treatment of renewable fuels to offset additional costs. [71517/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Tax policy is a matter for my colleague the Minister of Finance, and any queries the Deputy may have in relation to the treatment of excise and carbon tax should be addressed to the Department of Finance in the first instance.

As part of the Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO) development and design process, my Department completed two phases of analysis which included a full impact assessment on the scheme structure, considering critical factors, including the availability of renewable fuels to meet the obligation, the likely economic and social impact of the obligation, and resulting costs to end consumers. Detail in relation to each phase of analysis, including the full assessment carried out on potential obligation rates, is now available at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-climate-energy-and-the-environment/publications/renewable-heat-obligation/

Introduction of the RHO is a key objective for me, with priority drafting of the Renewable Heat Obligation Bill 2025 now underway. Once finalised in early 2026, I intend to submit the Renewable Heat Obligation Bill, along with any further information in relation to obligation rates and consumer costs, for Government approval to publish.

question.p: 188. Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on the legislative timeline for the Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO), including expected enactment and commencement dates; and whether contingency plans exist if the 2026 start date proves unachievable. [71518/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Introduction of the Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO) is a key objective for me, as Minister. Priority drafting of the RHO Bill 2025 is now underway with an expected completion date in early 2026. Once finalised, I intend to submit the final scheme for Government approval to publish and to ensure its timely enactment in 2026.

question.p: 189. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide the weekly application numbers for County Clare for the warmer homes scheme from 2021 to 2025, in tabular form. [71524/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Warmer Homes Scheme aims to improve the energy efficiency and warmth of homes owned by people at risk of energy poverty by providing fully funded retrofits. The scheme is operated by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) on behalf of my Department and is funded through carbon tax receipts and the European Regional Development Fund.
The specific information requested by the Deputy relates to operational matters and is not routinely supplied by the SEAI to my Department. It is suggested that the Deputy contact the SEAI directly.

The SEAI has established a specific email address for queries from Oireachtas members so that such queries can be addressed promptly and in line with the SEAI’s objective to deliver services to the highest standards. The email address is oireachtas@seai.ie.

question.p: 190. Deputy Michael Fitzmaurice asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will commit to incorporating a provision in the renewal of Ministerial approval for a group (details supplied) that will compel the approved body to establish and implement a mechanism for payment of the net necessary cost of collection and recycling to any RMO that can verifiably demonstrate the processing of obligated farm plastic, subject to an audited validation process, thereby ensuring a fair return for all market participants who contribute to national compliance targets; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71578/25]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Under the Waste Management (Farm Plastics) Regulations 2001, producers of farm plastic products must establish a deposit and refund scheme for farm plastic waste or participate in an approved compliance scheme for the recovery and recycling of this waste stream.

Since the introduction of the farm plastics extended producer responsibility (EPR) model, producers have opted to participate in the compliance scheme which is run by the Irish Farm Film Producers' Group (IFFPG). IFFPG is a not-for-profit organisation owned by its producer members and the IFA, operating under Ministerial Approval.

IFFPG manages the collection and recycling of farm plastic waste on behalf of its members and funds its operations from producer fees and collection charges. The setting of fees and charges, as well as commercial arrangements for the collection and recycling of this waste stream, are operational matters for IFFPG and its Board.

An application for approval to act as a compliance scheme for farm plastic waste has been submitted by IFFPG and is currently being assessed. As per the 2001 Regulations, IFFPG’s performance regarding measures taken and effects of these measures with regard to the recovery of farm plastic waste, achievement of targets, and nature and frequency of information provided to the Department and the financial stability of the Scheme, are all under consideration as part of this process.

question.p: 191. Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the way in which the National Marine Planning Framework ensures that the full picture of all activities in our national marine space are considered when drafting and designating the locations of marine protection areas. [71677/25]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The National Marine Planning Framework (NMPF) brings together all marine-based human activities for the first time, outlining Government’s vision, objectives and marine planning policies for each marine activity. The NMPF details how these marine activities will interact with each other in an ocean space that is under increasing spatial pressure, ensuring the sustainable use of our marine resources to 2040. The NMPF also outlines the supporting actions the Government considers necessary to effectively manage marine activities across the NMPF’s environmental, economic, and social pillars.

This NMPF is a key consideration for decision makers on all marine authorisations or applications for activity and development in Ireland’s maritime area, including those made within the new plan-led development system legislated for under the Maritime Area Planning Act 2021. Public decision making bodies are statutorily obliged to consider proposals in terms of their consistency with the objectives set out in the NMPF. The NMPF provides the overarching marine planning structure to ensure that decision making is consistent, evidence-based and focused on the sustainable future of our maritime area.

The decision to transfer the marine environment function from the Department of Housing Local Government and Heritage allows us to integrate the vital policy strands of maritime planning, sustainable use and protection of the marine environment. By doing this, we are able to plan and implement all the activities we need in our marine space in a sustainable manner while achieving and maintaining Good Environmental Status in our seas as required by the Marine Strategy Framework Directive so that they are clean, healthy and productive.

Marine protected areas (MPAs) are part of the toolkit we can use to ensure that we meet this environmental goal. The expansion of Ireland’s MPA network will take account of maritime spatial planning needs and socioeconomic and cultural interests in the maritime area. As part of the MPA process so far, there has been extensive engagement with stakeholders, sectors and the wider public. It is envisaged that such engagement and participation will be a cornerstone of MPA delivery into the future, supported by the MPA LIFE Ireland project and the wider work of the Department.

The proposed Maritime Area Protection (Marine Protected Areas Amendment) Bill will allow for the designation of MPAs by using Designated Maritime Area Plan process. This will provide for full stakeholder and public consultation for this designation process on a statutory basis.

question.p: 192. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide an update on the timeline for publishing the heads of bill for the private wires legislation. [71754/25]
193. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether he will seek a waiver for pre legislative scrutiny of the private wires legislation. [71758/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 192 and 193 together.
Having received Government approval for the Private Wires Policy Statement in July this year, my Department has initiated the process of drafting the subsequent necessary Private Wires legislation.
The General Scheme received Government approval this week. The Heads of Bill along with the Regulatory Impact Assessment will shortly be published on the Department’s website.
A waiver for pre legislative scrutiny will not be sought.

summary.i: Question No. 193 answered with Question No. 192.

question.p: 194. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether he has received reports from electricity network operators of outages from fluctuations in frequencies in the grid related to data centres causing issues; and the measures adopted to mitigate their effects. [71756/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment (Deputy Darragh O'Brien)
speech.p: EirGrid (Ireland’s Transmission System Operator (TSO)) and SONI (Northern Ireland’s TSO) are responsible for operating and developing the respective transmission systems of Ireland and Northern Ireland in a secure and coordinated manner, while also strategically planning for long-term electricity needs. System frequency deviations occur for a wide range of reasons and on an on-going basis. These are proactively managed by the System Operator to maintain system stability. Frequency disturbances associated with Data Centres largely arise as a result of how these demand units respond to other faults on the System.

EirGrid has proposed a Grid Code Modification to ensure that Data Centres improve how they respond to faults on the system which will in turn reduce frequency fluctuations related to Data Centres. My Department has supported this process through facilitated workshops with Industry and are actively engaging with EirGrid and CRU on this matter. The Grid Code Modification is due to be submitted to the CRU in Jan 2026.

question.p: 195. Deputy Eoin Ó Broin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the number of islanded data centres contracted to connect to the gas network; the number connected to the gas network of those contracted; the number awaiting connection to the gas network of those contracted; the number of formal enquiries that have been received but which are not contracted; and, for each category, the amount of capacity involved, in tabular form. [71755/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: It is understood that the term ‘islanded’ is intended to refer to a data centre fuelled mainly or wholly by fossil fuel and / or a data centre that does not have an electricity connection sufficient to cover its entire energy requirement.

I am advised that it is important to note that Gas Networks Ireland (GNI) does not assign or classify data centres as between “islanded” and “non-islanded”. The exact status of a data centre is primarily a function of the timelines (if any) pertaining to when that data centre will receive an electricity connection to allow them to move to electricity as their primary source.

The gas connection policy, and so GNI’s application process, does not currently require information as to alternative fuel sources and GNI does not formally collect information as to whether a data centre would be ‘islanded’ or indeed the anticipated duration of same.

GNI has provided the following information relating to the connection agreements entered into by GNI in relation to all data centres, together with information as to additional connection applications. This information relates to all formal applications for connection to GNI’s network, including so called ‘islanded’ data centres.

td.p: Data Centres contracted to connect to the gas network
Connected to the gas network (of those contracted)
Awaiting connection to the gas network (of those contracted)
Formal outstanding applications received from Data Centre Sites (but not contracted)

speech.p: *Of the 11 that are contracted, 7 are connected whereby 5 of those data centres connected are currently consuming gas

**Projected demand from these enquiries’ ranges from 40.5MW up to 1,300MW; the aggregated demand represents the total developer’s strategic long-term ambition which would be dependent on multiple factors including; ability to gain planning permission for multiple phases, availability of electricity grid capacity, permitting, data centre storage demand and route to market to fund these projects.

Government policy remains that ‘islanded’ data centres (that are not connected to the electricity grid and are powered mainly by on-site fossil fuel generation) would not be in line with national policy.

The new CRU connection policy focused on electricity connections and did not introduce any new decisions relating to connections to the gas network, however I am advised that CRU is actively engaging and will consult with GNI separately on this in the near term.

question.p: 196. Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the amount his Department has spent on translation services from a company (details supplied) for the years 2020 to 2025 to date, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72062/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: My Department has no record of using the services of the company identified during the specified timeframe.

summary.i: Question No. 197 answered with Question No. 181.

question.p: 198. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the total amount of battery storage available on the Irish electrical grid as of the latest figures; the capacity added in 2025 and the projected amount to be added in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72339/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Grid scale electricity storage systems including battery electricity storage systems play a vital role in Irelands energy transition by maximising the incorporation of renewable generated electricity, providing targeted demand flexibility to the grid, supporting grid build out and ensuring the proper functioning of the grid through system services.

As of November 2025, the system operators, EirGrid and ESB Networks, report that electricity storage systems with the capacity of 1,048 MW (megawatts) are connected to the grid network. One pumped hydro storage facility, Turlough Hill Co. Wicklow, accounts for 292 MW of this capacity with the remaining 756 MW provided by Stationary Battery Energy Storage Systems (S-BESS).
By comparison, approximately 4,350 MW of gas generation, 5,100 MW of wind generation and 2,100 MW of solar generation are connected to the grid network.

As of November, no additional electricity storage capacity have been reported as energised onto either the transmission or distribution grids in 2025, however, EirGrid currently has 28 storage projects totalling 1,698 MW with connection contracts pending fulfilment.
In support of Electricity Storage Systems, my Department published the Electricity Storage Policy Framework for Ireland in July 2024, which included 10 Government actions.

Action 6 of the policy framework supports the immediate procurement of 500 MW of Demand Flexibility Products by ESB Networks and 500 MW of Long Duration Electricity Storage (LDES) by EirGrid to meet specific network needs.
The first round of the ESB Networks Demand Flexibility Product, contracting 109MW of flexible capacity across 16 locations on to the distribution grid, is now live.

The EirGrid Long Duration Electricity Storage (LDES) product will incorporate electricity storage technologies with a minimum duration of 4 hours. The first contracts are expected to be signed in 2027, with the assets delivered by end of 2030.

question.p: 199. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the total amount of wind power generation on the Irish grid as of the latest figures; the capacity added in 2025; and the projected amount to be added in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72340/25]

200. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the total amount solar power generation on the Irish grid as of the latest figures; the capacity added in 2025; and the projected amount to be added in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72341/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 199 and 200 together.

The Programme for Government 2025 reaffirmed Ireland’s targets of 80% of electricity demand to be met by renewable energy sources, including a target of 9GW of onshore wind generation and 8 GW of solar generation as part of a strategy to decarbonise our power system.

SEAI has calculated the share of energy from renewable sources in gross final consumption of electricity was 41.4% in 2024, up from 40.4% in 2023. Furthermore, according to SEAI, over the last 12 months, 48.3% of indigenous electricity generation was from renewables.

EirGrid's Monthly Renewables Release for November provides provisional data showing 41% of electricity was generated from renewables, up from 34% in the same month last year. The majority of this renewable electricity came from wind with it accounting for 35% of all electricity used last month.

Ireland currently has circa 7.7 GW of installed renewable generation capacity, up from 1.2 GW in 2015. Onshore wind is the largest contributor with circa 5.1 GW of capacity. This is complemented by circa 1.7 GW of solar PV capacity, with Small-scale, Mini and Microgeneration, along with hydro, biomass, and other small sources contributing the remainder. Approximately 1.3 GW of this total has been added in 2025.

Government policy is focused on maintaining this momentum through 2026 and beyond as we deliver on the transition to a renewables led system. This will involve the development of a balanced portfolio of technologies, including solar, storage and flexibility services to complement other measures such as demand-side response, network development and interconnection to ensure a safe and secure electricity system with increased levels of renewables.
This will require unprecedented levels of investment in renewable electricity generation development and in the infrastructure required to expand and strengthen our electricity grid.

The Accelerating Renewable Electricity Taskforce was established to accelerate and increase the deployment of onshore renewable electricity generation by ensuring that barriers to the implementation of policies are removed or minimised to the greatest extent possible.

summary.i: Question No. 200 answered with Question No. 199.

question.p: 201. Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the projected additional power needs for data centres in 2026; if any recent analysis or report has been prepared for him, or within his Department, on the energy needs of data centres in Ireland in 2025 and projected for the next five years; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72342/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment (Deputy Darragh O'Brien)
speech.p: As the transmission system operator for Ireland, EirGrid is responsible for the operation and planning of the electricity transmission system. To achieve this, EirGrid must balance supply and demand now and forecast how to do so in the future. EirGrid’s All-Island Resource Adequacy Assessment looks at the balance between electricity demand and supply in Ireland for the next 10 years, which includes a ten-year demand forecast.

In EirGrid’s most recent published assessment, the All-Island Resource Adequacy Assessment 2025-2034, published in May 2025, the peak demand from the ramp-up of contracted data centres and new technology loads in 2025 is expected to be around 13% higher compared to the previous year, 2024. The same assessment indicates that peak demand from contracted data centres and new technology loads in 2026 is expected to be around 12% higher in 2026 compared to 2025. Over the next five years, i.e. from 2025 to 2030, peak demand from the ramp-up of contracted data centres and new technology loads is expected to grow by a cumulative 33%.

Ireland has attracted the best data centre and tech companies in the world. This is a really important relationship, and the Government continues to work with the sector towards a secure and decarbonised energy future. Data centres are central to Ireland’s economic and digital future as they are a key part of our value proposition for foreign direct investment and the associated employment and are central to Ireland’s economic and digital future.

summary.i: Question No. 202 answered with Question No. 180.
Question No. 203 answered with Question No. 180.

question.p: 204. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if Irish retail energy prices have fallen slower here than elsewhere in the EU; the measures he will take to address this; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72375/25]

205. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he is aware that Irish retail energy prices have fallen slower here than elsewhere in the EU; the work he has undertaken to discern the reasons for this; the measures he will take to address this; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72376/25]

206. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he is aware that the gap between wholesale and retail energy prices in Europe is widening; the work he has undertaken to discern the reasons for this; the measures he will take to address this; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72377/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 204 to 206, inclusive, together.

Regulation of retail energy markets is solely a matter for the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) since the enactment of the Electricity Regulation Act 1999, and subsequent legislation. The CRU is an independent regulator, accountable to the Oireachtas and not to me as Minister. However, officials from my Department engage with the CRU on an ongoing basis to track developments in the retail and wholesale energy markets.

The latest data from Eurostat shows that, in nominal terms, Ireland ranked fifth for electricity prices and eighth for household gas prices among European countries in the first half of 2025. When adjusting for purchasing power parity, Ireland is mid-table in terms of energy affordability with the twelfth highest electricity and gas prices among European countries.

The CRU published a report on retail energy markets in September 2023 in relation to competition and supplier pricing in the energy market. The report was in response to a request by the then Minister to examine supplier hedging practices and pricing strategies in the Irish energy market. Based on a review of supplier prices and wholesale market costs, the CRU considered that retail prices are broadly continuing to reflect underlying cost drivers, such as wholesale gas and electricity prices, but with a lag period due to supplier hedging strategies.

The CRU also published a report comparing household electricity and gas prices between Ireland and other European countries in 2024. This report outlined that hedging strategies employed by energy suppliers lessened the impact of price increases for households but resulted in elevated retail prices when compared to other European countries.

Under the Programme for Government 2025, we have committed to commissioning an independent review into the speed and level of pass through from wholesale prices to retail prices, with an additional assessment of the overall price dynamics and a focus on the competitiveness of the Irish economy. I have written to the CRU to commence work on this review and my officials have held initial discussions with the regulator in relation to progressing this commitment.

My Department has also established a cross-Government National Energy Affordability Taskforce to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses, while delivering key renewable commitments and protecting security of supply and economic stability.

The taskforce's first report set out measures for consideration as part of the Budget 2026 process. This report has been published on Gov.ie, in advance of further analysis and the publication of the Energy Affordability Action Plan in 2026.

summary.i: Question No. 205 answered with Question No. 204.
Question No. 206 answered with Question No. 204.

question.p: 207. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment his views on whether it will be helpful for the energy regulator to provide the arrears data on a monthly basis as has been recommended by the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Climate, Environment and Energy; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72378/25]

208. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he sought updated arrears data from the regulator in advance of the Budget; and if not, the reason he did not seek this data and if he would make; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72379/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 207 and 208 together.

The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) regularly publishes market monitoring data, including the estimated annual bills for households; the number of households in payment arrears on their energy bills; the number of disconnections; and the number of customers switching energy supplier. Arrears data is generally published by the CRU on a monthly basis, though it is acknowledged that there was a delay in the publication of the data in July, August and September of this year. As arrears data operates with a two-month time lag due to the way suppliers report these figures to the CRU and the need to validate the data, the latest published arrears figures are for September 2025.

The data show that there are currently 297,313 customers in electricity arrears. This is a 3.4% decrease from the August figure of 307,862. For those in arrears more than 90 days, 187,307 electricity customers were in arrears in September 2025, a slight decrease of 0.7% from August 2025 (188,618).

In relation to gas, 179,576 customers were in arrears in September 2025, a 3.8% decrease from 186,594 households in August. Regarding customers in arrears over 90 days, this stood at 153,658 in September, a decrease of 0.5% from August 2025.

The CRU is currently reviewing its market monitoring framework through which this data is collected and reported upon. The review aims to provide more granular information to gain a better understanding of the numbers of customers who may be in more distress and in need of support with their debt.

The Deputy may wish to engage directly with the CRU in relation to the matters raised. The CRU provides a dedicated email address, oireachtas@cru.ie, for Oireachtas members which enables them to raise questions on general energy regulatory matters.

summary.i: Question No. 208 answered with Question No. 207.

question.p: 209. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if the National Energy Affordability Taskforce has completed modelling on projected long-term electricity and gas arrears over the next year and over the next five years; if the modelling will be published; and the way in which this modelling will inform Government policy. [72381/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The National Energy Affordability Taskforce was established in June 2025 to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses. The first report of the taskforce was published last month. This report analysed recent trends in energy costs and related matters, including arrears, and set out a range of options for consideration as part of the Budget 2026 process. The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU), as a member of the taskforce, fed into the report and also presented data at a taskforce meeting in relation to prices, arrears and details of CRU customer protection measures. Minutes of the taskforce meetings are available at: www.gov.ie

The CRU and officials from my Department monitor arrears levels on an ongoing basis, as a key indicator in their tracking of retail energy markets. There are many variables, including those related to energy costs and the general health of the economy, which directly influence arrears levels and would make long-term arrears level forecasting particularly challenging.

The CRU is currently reviewing its market monitoring framework through which this data is collected and reported upon. The review aims to provide more granular information to gain a better understanding of the numbers of customers who may be in energy distress and in need of support with their debt. This analysis will inform the work of the taskforce going forward, which will include the development of targeted measures to assist households most vulnerable to energy cost pressures.

question.p: 210. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if he will publish an updated year-by-year trajectory to 2030 for renewable electricity generation, by onshore wind, offshore wind and solar PV capacity; the contingency measures he will introduce to stay on track to meet the 80% renewable electricity target; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72382/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: This Question was answered under Dáil Question number 287 of 11 December 2025 and the position remains the same.

The Programme for Government 2025 has reaffirmed Ireland’s targets of 80% of electricity demand to be met by renewable energy sources. Achieving this target not only depends on additional renewable electricity generation but also on deployment of electricity storage which plays a critical role in enabling higher levels of variable wind and solar on the system, supporting flexibility.

The updated National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) sets out the policies to be implemented to achieve our energy and climate targets and contains year-by-year trajectory to 2030 for each renewable electricity generation. The updated NECP is available on the following link: assets.gov.ie/static/documents/irelands-integrated-national-energy-and-climate-plan-2021-2030.pdf

Two cross-Government taskforces, the Accelerating Renewable Electricity Taskforce (ARET) for onshore renewables and the Offshore Wind Delivery Taskforce (OWDT), continue to develop effective policies designed to deliver an accelerated and increased level of renewable generation capacity and related infrastructure, including strengthening the electricity grid and increasing electricity storage.

Ireland has a number of support schemes in place to increase the development of renewable electricity. The Renewable Electricity Support Scheme (RESS) is pivotal to the achievement of Ireland’s 2030 target. RESS consists of a series of competitive auctions, five onshore and two offshore to date, in which successful applicants are offered a two-way support arrangement for a period of approximately 15 years. The Programme for Government committed that RESS auctions will take place annually, which provide a consistent pathway for the continued deployment of renewable electricity.

The revised National Planning Framework includes regional renewable electricity capacity allocations. The inclusion of the allocations will facilitate the accelerated roll-out and delivery of onshore wind and solar development.
Government remains committed to the development of 5 GW of offshore wind capacity with projects in construction by 2030 and energised as soon as feasible thereafter.

question.p: 211. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the analysis which has been done regarding the combined impact of the RHO and PR6 from January 2025; the amount by which he expects average bills will rise; the measures he will take to mitigate the impact to households; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72383/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Programme for Government acknowledges the increased energy cost pressures on households and businesses, and commits to bringing forward additional measures to address these costs. My Department has established a cross-Government Energy Affordability Taskforce to identify, assess and implement measures that will enhance energy affordability for households and businesses, while delivering key renewables commitments and protecting security of supply and economic stability. The taskforce has recently published an interim report, which sets out measures for consideration as part of the Budget 2026 process, and in advance of publication of the Energy Affordability Action Plan in 2026.

Ireland is committed to reaching a legally binding target of climate neutrality by no later than 2050, and a cut of 51% in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. As Ireland imports most of its fossil fuels, our heating sector is a significant contributor to Ireland’s high energy import dependency and carbon emissions, and introduction of the Renewable Heat Obligation (RHO) is a key objective for me, as Minister, to address these challenges.

Given the potential impact the RHO could have on end consumers, energy affordability and the impact on household energy bills were key considerations in developing the scheme. My Department has carried out extensive analysis and stakeholder engagement activities, including with energy suppliers, to ensure final decisions taken in relation to the scheme are evidence-based and supportive of its successful introduction. A number of scheme parameters have been designed to allow flexibility to obligated parties in meeting their obligations, which will in turn reduce the overall burden on the end consumer. Detail in relation to each phase of analysis, including the full assessment carried out on potential obligation rates, and resulting impact on end consumers is available at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-climate-energy-and-the-environment/publications/renewable-heat-obligation/

Responsibility for the regulation of the electricity market and implementation of the PR6 process and its outcomes is a matter for the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU). The CRU is an independent regulator and, in relation to the outcome of the price review strategy and associated issues, the Deputy may wish to engage with them directly. However, the Deputy should note the significant equity investment that the Government is making in the System Operators. EirGrid is to receive an investment of €2 billion and ESB an investment of €1.5 billion. This will strengthen their balance sheets and allow them to finance their investments under PR6 at the lowest possible interest rates which will minimise the ultimate cost to consumers of these essential investments.

question.p: 212. Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment his views regarding energy cloud; if he has considered including the use of surplus energy as part of the Government's retrofit programme; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72384/25]

220. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the total volume of renewable electricity that was dispatched down or curtailed in each of the past five years; the estimated financial value of this wasted energy; and the actions being taken to ensure this surplus is redirected for productive social use, particularly for households in fuel poverty; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72531/25]

221. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his Department plans to introduce mandatory obligations on system operators, suppliers or aggregators to capture and utilise surplus renewable electricity for social benefit; if not, the rationale for this; and whether he accepts that the continued waste of clean energy during an energy poverty crisis; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72532/25]

222. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the full extent of engagement between his Department, the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland, EirGrid, ESB Networks and a company (details supplied); whether a formal service-level or funding agreement is under consideration; if he will commit to supporting a national rollout of the company's model; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72533/25]

224. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment whether his Department will develop a matched-funding model with corporate energy users, similar to a pilot (details supplied), to scale the redirection of surplus wind power into social housing and low-income private homes nationwide; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72535/25]

225. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the reason more than 300 days after the Programme for Government commitment to use surplus renewable energy to support those in fuel poverty, no national delivery framework has been published; the person or body which holds responsibility for this delay; and when a statutory delivery plan will be brought to Cabinet; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72536/25]

226. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the changes to market design or network charging which are being advanced to ensure that surplus renewable electricity is treated first as a social resource for heat and domestic energy, rather than as a by-product absorbed by curtailment; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72537/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 212, 220 to 222, inclusive, and 224 to 226, inclusive, together.

Imperfections and dispatch down is a major challenge facing electricity systems, like ours, that are increasingly powered by renewables. This complex issue can only be addressed by taking a systematic and multi-faceted approach requiring investment in grid, storage and demand flexibility.

We are already taking steps to invest in this critical energy infrastructure. For example, PR6 will enable the delivery of over 500 capital network projects, supporting the integration of increasing volumes of renewables and helping to reduce the amount of wasted energy. In July, the Government committed to investing €3.5 billion of NDP funding in EirGrid and ESB Networks in order to ensure that the PR6 infrastructure programme can be delivered. Legislation providing the legal mechanism necessary for the investment of €1.5 billion of this funding into ESBN has now passed all stages and was signed into law by the President last month. Further legislation in relation to the investment in Eirgrid will be progressed next year.

Last year, my Department published the Electricity Storage Policy Framework for Ireland which supported the procurement of 500 MW of demand flexibility products by ESBN and 500 MW of long duration electricity storage by EirGrid to meet specific network needs. Work is already underway to ensure the timely delivery of both.

In June, EirGrid established the Renewable Dispatch Down Working Group. This group is actively working with renewable industry representatives to identify additional actions that could improve levels of ‘dispatch down’.

Demand flexibility can also help to support our transition to a renewables-led energy system. The National Energy Demand Strategy aims to make 20% to 30% of electricity demand flexible by 2030. A key aspect of this strategy is preparing households and businesses to maximise their use of renewables.

The National Energy Affordability Taskforce was established by my Department to identify and assess measures to enhance energy affordability for households and businesses. The first report of the taskforce was published last month with an Energy Affordability Action Plan to be prepared next year. The taskforce will progress the Programme for Government commitment raised by the Deputy and the action plan will incorporate measures to further address 'dispatch down'.

Officials from my Department and the SEAI have met representatives from Energy Cloud on several occasions, and will continue to engage widely to support innovative mechanisms for benefitting households in energy poverty as part of the taskforce work programme.

question.p: 213. Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the progress of the Electricity (Supply) (Amendment) Bill 2025; the measures it contains to enhance Ireland's storm preparedness; when he expects it to be read at second stage in Dail Éireann; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72424/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The Electricity (Supply) (Amendment) Bill 2025 is being progressed by my Department as part of a wider programme of work to strengthen the resilience of Ireland’s electricity network in the context of climate change and increasingly severe storm events. A central objective of the Bill is to support enhanced storm preparedness through improved management of the interaction between forestry and the electricity network. Local communities cannot be expected to endure major storm impacts through the loss of power caused by trees falling on the network. In this context, the Bill and associated policy measures are underpinned by key strands of work outlined below.

Firstly, work is underway on the development of an enduring electricity corridor design. This is being informed by an international review of best practice in forestry corridor management, forestry design standards, and structured stakeholder engagement.

Secondly, the Bill will provide for electricity corridors to be placed on a statutory footing. This will safeguard electricity corridors in all new forestry development and will support the retrospective creation of corridors in existing forestry, using a risk-based approach delivered through a phased, multi-year programme.

Thirdly, an annual corridor clearance programme has been established by ESB Networks. Detailed surveys of overhead line corridors have already provided a strong evidence base on windblow risk. This information will be used to prioritise an annual, multi-year corridor clearance programme, targeted at those locations presenting the highest risk to customer resilience from forestry-related outages.
The overarching objective is to ensure that overhead electricity networks and forestry can co-exist in a manner that delivers a secure and reliable electricity supply.

The Government approved the Heads of this Bill in July and work on advancing the legislation continues as a matter of priority with a view to publication at the earliest opportunity. Once approved for publication, arrangements will be made for second stage and its passage through the Oireachtas.

question.p: 214. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment to provide further details on the updated scientific advice, which he received in November 2025, showing that Lough Corrib SAC salmon stocks will not have a sustainable surplus available for harvest in 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72488/25]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The scientific catch advice on salmon fisheries for the 2026 season is provided by the Technical Expert Group on Salmon (TEGOS). The TEGOS Report is available on Inland Fisheries Ireland’s website at www.fisheriesireland.ie/publications.

Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI) have advised that the stock assessment and associated catch advice given for the Corrib is primarily based on the fish counter at the Galway Weir and uses the most recent five-year period of data (i.e. 2021-2025). The counter is a partial counter so the raw count data is doubled. Ranched salmon passing through the counter are removed from the estimates of the run as the stock assessment and catch advice is based on wild salmon. Harvest of wild salmon below the counter are added to the counter run to get a full estimate of returns of salmon to the river. Essentially the average of the five years of the stock estimate is used to forecast the number of adults that will return to the river for the upcoming season (i.e. 2026).

Using five-years of data ensures that a single very good or bad year doesn’t over or under-estimate the forecast. It also generally reflects the life cycle period of salmon. The forecasted number of adults that return is then compared to the conservation limit for the river (i.e. minimum number of returning fish a river requires to ensure its stock remains healthy) and any returns above this are considered surplus to the health of the stock and thus available for sustainable harvest.

A level of certainty is required that the conservation limit will be achieved at the surplus quota advised to account for the risks in the catch advice. The standard basis for the stock assessment and associated catch advice provides for a high probability (i.e. 75% chance) that the conservation limit will be met by the forecasted returns at the quota set. IFI have decided that more certainty is warranted (i.e. 85% probability that the conservation limit will be met at the quota advised) over the base scientific advice. This reduces the quota that would be otherwise advised.

At the 85% probability level, no quota for sustainable harvest is available and as such catch and release-only fishing is advised for this stock in 2026. This better aligns with North Atlantic Salmon Conservation Organisation advice that stock exploitation should not solely be managed to the standard conservation limits themselves but should also have management targets above this to build in an extra level of precaution. These precautions are deemed necessary in the context of the uncertain future trajectory of our salmon stocks in general which have continued to progressively decline in Ireland in recent decades. Such an approach is also considered necessary to uphold the long-term term viability of the stock in the context of the many threats and pressures this species continues to be subject to.

question.p: 215. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his Department will continue to validate the presence of invasive/non-native fish such as pike, roach and carp in the Corrib Catchment through conservation bye-laws considering his comments on 4 December 2025 regarding significant coarse fisheries within the catchment; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72489/25]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI) have advised that coarse fish and pike have been present in the Lough Corrib catchment for many years. IFI regularly monitor fish populations in several waterbodies in the Lough Corrib Catchment to assess their composition, abundance, age structure and ecological status. Lough Corrib, along with six other large freshwater lakes in the west of Ireland are currently being managed preferentially as recreational salmonid fisheries and the information gathered through IFI surveys is used as an ecological indicator and to inform fishery management decisions. Coarse fish and pike stocks are managed at some locations.

The conservation bye-laws referred to in the question, which currently underpin the protection and management of coarse fish in Ireland, are currently under review. A public consultation process has recently closed and I look forward to the review process concluding in due course.

question.p: 216. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if the proposed Western Lakes Management Plan (WLMP) facilitates further promotion of coarse angling on Lough Corrib SAC and its catchment; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72490/25]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I have been advised by Inland Fisheries Ireland that the promotion of angling is outside the proposed Western Lakes Management Plan. While the plan includes management options for all fish species that are present, it is not an angling promotion plan. Anglers will, however, play an important role as stakeholders in the implementation and success of the plan.

question.p: 217. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment if his Department will be instigating any legislative or policy changes as a result of the public consultation that ended recently regarding the Conservation of Pike Bye-Law (No. 809) 2006 and the Conservation and Prohibition on Sale of Coarse Fish Bye-Law (No. 806) 2006; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72492/25]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: A review process is underway in relation to the Conservation of Pike Bye-Law (No. 809) 2006 and the Conservation and Prohibition on Sale of Coarse Fish Bye-Law (No. 806) 2006.

A public consultation process, to inform the review, was completed by Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI) in November. The 214 submissions received are being analysed and IFI intends to publish copies of these submissions on its website in early January.

I look forward to the review process concluding in due course. I will consider the advice and recommendations brought forward by IFI before deciding whether legislative or policy changes are required.

question.p: 218. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the number of departmental officials that have held the post of principal officer of the Inland Fisheries Division since 1 January 2015; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72495/25]

speech.from: Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: I can confirm to the Deputy that the number of officials in my Department at principal officer level who have held the post with responsibility for Inland Fisheries since 1 January 2015 is three.

question.p: 219. Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment the reason the Suir River in the Waterford fishery district will remain open for salmon angling in 2026 on a ‘catch and release’ basis considering that there is a known mortality with releasing fish alive after handling as per peer reviewed literature; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72496/25]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment
speech.p: The conservation limit (CL), applied by the Technical Expert Group on Salmon (TEGOS), to establish the status of individual stocks is the “maximum sustainable yield” (MSY) (also known as the stock level that maximises the long-term average surplus) as defined and used by the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) and the North Atlantic Salmon Conservation Organisation (NASCO).

The CL is essentially the minimum number of returning salmon a river requires to ensure its stock remains healthy. In the absence of an advised surplus on a river, ‘Catch and Release only’ options are proposed for rivers meeting between 65% -100% of their CL for 2026 in line with scientific advice.

The harvesting of salmon is only permitted in stocks in rivers or associated estuaries which are above their CL, so that any harvest quota set will ensure that a stock is fished sustainably without impacting the viability of that stock.

The River Suir is currently below its CL and falls into the 65% -100% bracket and therefore it is proposed that it will be Catch and Release only for the 2026 season. The management recommendation, following the TEGOS advice for the last number of years on the River Suir, is for a catch and release regime. This is because there is not a surplus available for harvest.

Ireland manages its salmon populations on a river-by-river basis based on robust conservation-focused scientific advice. This is based on scientific stock assessments and associated sustainable catch advice provided by the independent TEGOS. Our salmon management regime follows international best practice as advised by the NASCO and ICES.

Estimates of direct catch and release caused-mortalities in Atlantic salmon vary between individual studies, with values ranging from as low as 3% mortality to as high as 40% mortality. Numerous interacting factors can influence the reported mortality rate including gear/angling technique (e.g. barbless or barbed hook, fly or lure, play time, air-exposure time) and life-stage (grilse, multi-sea winter, kelt) with higher water temperature consistently emerges as a major factor controlling mortality probability.

To date, the lethal and sub-lethal effects of catch and release angling have not directly been accounted for in the Irish salmon stock assessment and catch advice process. However, it is important to note that the current catch advice provided by TEGOS gives a measure of protection to particularly vulnerable river stocks (i.e. those meeting 65% of their conservation limit) by advising that no recreational fisheries should operate and thus such stocks are fully protected from any potential negative effects of catch and release as outlined above when the scientific thresholds are adhered to. In general, facilitating catch and release-only fishing on stocks somewhat below their CL, generates valuable catch data that can be used for stock assessment purposes which otherwise may not be available while also providing a socio-economic benefit.

The proposed salmon fisheries management measures for the 2026 season are currently available for Public Consultation. The Public Consultation process, conducted by my Department, is open for 30 days so as to allow stakeholder who have a vested interest review and submit comments during this period.
