question.p: 1147. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Health the key measures taken to improve cancer care during 2025; her priorities for same in 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72565/25]

speech.from: Minister for Health (Deputy Jennifer Carroll MacNeill)
speech.p: Funding of €27.4 billion has been allocated to the health service for 2026, an increase of 6.2%. Next year, a new approach is being taken to funding allocation with health budgets being devolved to the HSE regions, giving them greater autonomy to meet local needs while holding them accountable for ambitious targets and national standards.

The National Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) will continue to lead on service design nationally and the implementation of the National Cancer Strategy. The NCCP also monitors performance and works closely with the regions to ensure the delivery of safe, effective cancer services.

I am continuing to work towards the delivery of multi-annual budgets in health over the coming years. Capital investment already operates multi-annually and it is a priority for me to introduce this across all areas of the budget.

Since its launch in July 2017, the Government has allocated €105 million to the National Cancer Strategy to support cancer services and improve outcomes for patients. Since then, very significant progress has been made in improving cancer services. There are now over 220,000 people living with or beyond cancer, 50% more than a decade ago.

One in two people are expected to receive a cancer diagnosis in their lifetime. We are seeing tremendous advances in cancer care and I am committed to ensuring that patients can take advantage of these developments. Work will begin shortly on an evaluation of the Cancer Strategy which will inform the development of a new strategy next year.

question.p: 1148. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Health the key measures taken to improve screening services during 2025; her priorities for same in 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72566/25]

speech.p: As this is a service matter, it has been referred to the Health Service Executive for attention and direct reply to the Deputy.

question.p: 1149. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Health the key measures taken to improve pharmacy services during 2025; her priorities for same in 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72567/25]

speech.p: In 2025, measures to improve pharmacy services included the introduction of the Hormone Replacement Therapy Arrangement, which commenced on 1 June 2025, and the enabling of the introduction of a Common Conditions Service (CCS), which will enable pharmacists to provide treatment for eight specified common conditions. Further information on the CCS can be found at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/press-releases/minister-for-health-signs-legislation-that-will-enable-pharmacists-to-prescribe-for-certain-common-conditions-for-the-first-time/

The Community Pharmacy Agreement 2025 was agreed between the Department of Health (DoH), the Health Service Executive (HSE), and the Irish Pharmacy Union (IPU) on 12 September 2025, and published on 18 September 2025. It sets out a comprehensive and ongoing pathway to modernise and expand the role of community pharmacy in Ireland’s healthcare system. The Agreement is designed to support the delivery of safe, equitable, and efficient healthcare, and to ensure that community pharmacists are better equipped to contribute to national health priorities through structured engagement, sustainable funding, and integrated service delivery. The Agreement will be implemented on a phased basis and will be supported by regular structured engagements between the Department, HSE and the IPU. The continuation of a high-level, enduring strategic relationship is designed to support the shaping and implementation of pharmacy’s role in a more integrated, efficient, and patient-centred health system. Under the Agreement, a Strategic Collaboration Group will be established which will provide a structured forum for dialogue and joint consideration of strategic issues shaping the future of community pharmacy in Ireland.The full text of the Community Pharmacy Agreement 2025 can be found at: www.gov.ie/en/department-of-health/publications/community-pharmacy-agreement-2025/

question.p: 1150. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Health the key measures taken to improve social care services during 2025; her priorities for same in 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72568/25]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Health (Deputy Jennifer Murnane O'Connor)
speech.p: I thank the Deputy for his clarification of the wording of this question, "To ask the Minister for Health the key measures taken to improve homelessness services and addiction services during 2025; her priorities for same in 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter."

In 2025, €56m in funding was allocated to the HSE to provide targeted health and social care services for people who are homeless – this will increase in 2026, with at least an extra €3.53m being allocated to the HSE for homeless health services in the coming year.

As the Deputy is aware, people who are homelessness are likely to experience severe health inequalities. They experience a high prevalence of physical disease, mental illness, and substance use. There are also more likely to die prematurely. Homelessness undermines the effectiveness of health care services by creating additional barriers for people in accessing treatment in a timely and integrated manner. For all these reasons, increased provision of health services to people who are homeless is a priority for me and for the Dept of Health and a number of measures are ongoing in this regard.

The success of the integrated assertive case management teams (PACT teams) in Dublin, with almost 6,000 cases receiving case management since the inception of the service in September 2022, will be further built on in 2026. Funding has been approved for an expansion of the service in Dublin and establishment of the service outside of the Dublin area, thereby ensuring consistent and equitable access to integrated care and case management across the health regions.

In July 2025, the Dept of Health and the HSE agreed to further increase in the capacity of the Community Care and Treatment Facility at Usher’s Island from 51 to 63 beds. This brings to €8.5m the combined Dept of Health and HSE investment in the facility to-date and is the largest investment by the Dept in healthcare services for people who are homeless.

A key strategic priority of the National Drugs Strategy is to enhance access to, and delivery of, drugs services in the community. Demand for and access to services has increased during the period of the current national drugs strategy.

The Department of Health allocated over €176 million under the National Drug Strategy in 2024 for the provision of addiction services. As part of Budget 2026, I announced an additional €11 million in recurring funding for drugs and inclusion health services to progress priority measures. This includes €4 million for service enhancement measures and will address regional disparities in availability of drug and inclusion health services, with a strong focus on the provision of services in disadvantaged and rural areas.

Data published in the 2024 National Drug Treatment Reporting System (NDTRS) by the Health Research Board (HRB) shows that there was a record figure of 13,295 cases treated for problem drug use in 2024. This continues the upward trend in treatment cases and demonstrates the impact of the National Drugs Strategy in enhancing access to drug services, with an increase of 50% in cases since the strategy began in 2017.

The additional funding provide for drug and inclusion health services in Budget 2026 demonstrate my strong commitment as Minister to meeting the health needs of people who are homeless and those who use drugs or who use alcohol in a harmful way.

question.p: 1151. Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Health the key measures taken to support and improve GP services during 2025; her priorities for same in 2026; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [72569/25]

speech.p: As per the Programme for Government, the Government is committed to increasing the number of GPs practicing across in the State, thereby improving access to GP services for all patients. Increasing our GP workforce, primarily through a combination of international recruitment and increased training places, is among the priorities in this regard for this year and next year. Annual investment provided for general practice has been increased by over €340 million under the 2019 and 2023 GP Agreements. The agreements provide for increased GP capitation fees, increased and new supports for practices, as well as new fees for additional services. The 2023 Agreement also provided for the expansion of GP visit card eligibility to all children under 8 years of age and to all those who earn up to median household income.

The implementation of both Agreements continues, increasing the attractiveness of working in general practice in Ireland. As per the 2023 Agreement, a new locum support initiative commenced in May this year which provides GPs in receipt of rural practice supports with access to a streamlined locum sourcing service. The annual intake of doctors into the GP training programme has been increased by approximately 80% from 2019 to 2024, with 350 new entrant training places made available in 2024 and again in 2025. The number of new entrant training places is to increase again next year by 50 places to 400. As a result, the number of GP graduates has increased in recent years and will continue to increase in the coming years. Having commenced in 2023, recruitment of GPs from abroad is ongoing under the International Medical Graduate (IMG) Rural GP Programme.

Significant funding was provided for this year to allow for continued and increased recruitment under the programme. As of end of Q3, there are 115 IMG GPs within the programme currently placed in general practice and a further 39 have completed the 2-year programme. The placement of IMG GPs is targeted to rural and underserved areas. Further potential measures to support GP practices are being considered under the Strategic Review of General Practice. With input from key stakeholders, the review is examining the broad range of issues affecting general practice. Following its completion, a final report will be presented to me outlining the findings of the review and setting out recommended actions for a more sustainable general practice.

question.p: 1152. Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Health the arrangements that are in place to ensure every GP in Ireland is trained in the latest understanding and teachings on Menopause; the number of GPs licensed to practice in Ireland, by county; and the number of GPs who have completed menopause training in the past 12 months, by county, in tabular form. [72572/25]

speech.p: The Women’s Health Action Plans 2022-2023 and 2024-2025, together with significant Government investment, have resulted in important improvements to women’s health services in Ireland. The work of the Women’s Health Taskforce and the implementation of these Action Plans have also increased awareness of many women’s health issues, both among the public and amongst healthcare professionals. Much work has been done to support women through their menopause journeys we have progressed various initiatives to enhance holistic and clinician supports available to women at both primary and acute levels. These include:
• A GP Clinical Lead for Women’s Health established 2021, to lead on the improvement of women’s health supports in the community.
• The development of a menopause theory course for GPs and GP trainees via the Irish College of General Practitioners.

• The development of a Quick Reference Guide on Menopause for GPs in 2022. The guide comprises of evidence-based information on the management of perimenopause and menopause in general practice by GPs and practice nurses.

• The launch, also in 2022, of a National Menopause Awareness campaign. This was a direct response to the demand from Irish women for greater knowledge and understanding of menopause as well as better access to accurate information and supports. A second phase of the campaign was relaunched in 2023 as part of the Department of Health’s Women’s Health Week.
• The launch of a dedicated webpage to provide trusted information for anyone affected by menopause in Ireland – gov.ie/menopause

• Six dedicated Specialist Menopause Clinics are open and operational for women who require complex, specialist care. Additional funding was provided under Phase 2 of the Women’s Health Action Plan to extend the provision of services in 4 of the Specialist Menopause Clinics.

• Since 1 June 2025, Hormone Replace Therapy for the management of the symptoms of menopause is now free, lowering the cost burden of menopause for women in Ireland. As the ICGP is body responsible for GP training and GP continual professional development, the Department of Health does not maintain a register of the number of GPs who have completed menopause training. As information on the number of GPs practising medicine by county is an operational matter, I have asked the HSE to reply to the Deputy in relation to that as soon as possible.

question.p: 1153. Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the financial supports available to students from Gaza who are accepted into programmes in Irish universities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71333/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: The Irish Palestine Scholarship Programme (IPSP) is part of the Ireland Fellows global scholarship programme run by the Government of Ireland providing opportunities for candidates to choose from a wide variety of courses at 19 higher education institutions in Ireland. The Ireland Fellows Programme, which is delivered by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, is a longstanding international development initiative grounded in the belief that education is central to creating a better world and fostering long-term sustainable change. The programmes leverages Ireland's world-class higher education institutions to empower individuals from eligible developing countries, enabling them to acquire advanced skills and knowledge that they can apply upon returning home

Further details of the IPSP including the operation of the application and selection process, the number of available places and the supports available to successful applicants can be found at: www.ireland.ie/en/ramallah/about/ireland-palestine-scholarship-programme/#about

question.p: 1154. Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the reason students are only eligible for the Christmas bonus if they are receiving VTOS or Youthreach training allowance for at least 12 months, or if they were receiving a qualified payment immediately before their training, considering not all VTOS or Youthreach students apply for another qualifying payment for the months they are not in education; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71364/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: My Department is committed to breaking down cost barriers, making Further Education and Training (FET) more accessible than ever before. To date in 2025, my Department has spent over €57 million on training allowances to support the engagement and success of eligible learners who face financial barriers in FET. This figure excludes apprenticeship state allowances and allowances paid to learners in Specialist Training Providers.

SOLAS's FET Learner Allowances Policy sets out that the eligibility criteria for the Christmas Bonus is determined by the Department of Social Protection (DSP). The bonus is payable to long-term social welfare recipients and certain training allowance recipients who meet the qualifying conditions set out by that Department. Where a learner was in receipt of a qualifying DSP payment immediately before commencing their FET course, the time spent on that payment can be combined with the time on the training allowance to meet the 12-month requirement.

In the case of VTOS participants, most learners have been in receipt of a qualifying social welfare payment prior to joining the programme and retain an underlying entitlement when they transfer to a VTOS training allowance. As a result, they are more likely to meet the eligibility criteria for the Christmas Bonus, provided they have been on a qualifying payment or training allowance for at least 12 months.

Youthreach learners, on the other hand, are generally aged between 16 and 18 and do not have an underlying social welfare entitlement. Consequently, they are unlikely to qualify for the Christmas Bonus. For those who join Youthreach at age 18, eligibility requires that they have an underlying social welfare entitlement and meet the qualifying conditions set by the DSP.

question.p: 1155. Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to consider aligning the Youthreach calendar year with the second level calendar year; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71365/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: By way of background for the Deputy, Youthreach provides a two-year education and training pathway for young people who have left mainstream education with limited qualifications. The programme supports learners in gaining the skills, knowledge, and confidence to progress to further education, training, or employment. Certification is typically achieved at Levels 3 and 4 on the National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ).

In 2023, the Teachers’ Union of Ireland (TUI) requested that the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) recommence conciliation on a previously submitted claim that sought alignment of the 225-day Youthreach calendar with that of the post-primary school calendar. My Department has been engaging with the TUI on this and agreed on a structured approach to consider the proposal. As part of this process, officials have undertaken a comprehensive data collection exercise, consulted with key stakeholders, and analysed the data gathered. Officials are currently finalising a paper, which I expect to receive for consideration in the coming weeks. Given the significance of the proposed changes to the delivery of this important national programme, I am sure the Deputy will agree that, in considering TUI’s proposal, a thorough and evidence-informed process is essential.

question.p: 1156. Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if information will be provided on the results of the Standardisation of Youthreach Calendar Year Sectoral Survey of ETBs; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71366/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: I can confirm that my Department did not issue the Standardisation of Youthreach Calendar Year Sectoral Survey. This survey was conducted by Education and Training Boards Ireland (ETBI) to inform a submission to my Department’s work to consider the Teachers’ Union of Ireland claim seeking alignment of the Youthreach academic calendar year with that of the post-primary school academic year. If the Deputy requires further information on the survey or its results, I would advise contacting ETBI directly.

question.p: 1157. Deputy John McGuinness asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the number of apprentices undertaking courses at a centre (details supplied); the type of apprenticeships offered; the number of applicants for each course in each of the past four years; the number of full time clerical staff involved in the administration of the courses and their qualifications; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71422/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: At present, Tipperary FET College Carrick-on-Suir provides training for the Electrical programme at Phase 2. Apprenticeship provision began at the centre in September 2024. As such, it is only possible to provide data commencing from that date. As of 10 December, 70 electrical apprentices have already gone through training at Tipperary FET College Carrick-on-Suir, and an additional 28 apprentices are currently undertaking training there.

In compliance with GDPR legislation, it is not possible to provide detailed information regarding the specific qualifications held by individuals. Programme training is provided by three Electrical instructors, each with a minimum of a Level 6 National Craft Certificate and a minimum of five years' experience. The centre employs two clerical staff - one full-time and one part-time - who are responsible for the administration of all FET provision within the centre.

question.p: 1158. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the status of the TrustEd assessments of language schools; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71477/25]

1159. Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the number of approved English language schools in Ireland; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71478/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1158 and 1159 together.

I propose to take questions 71477 and 71478 together.The provision of English language education in Ireland is a broad and diverse sector with the vast majority of activity undertaken by privately owned education providers. While my Department does not collate data on English language schools, it is estimated that there are approximately over 100 English language schools currently operating in Ireland. Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI), an agency under the remit of my Department, is currently introducing TrustEd Ireland – a new international education quality mark. TrustEd Ireland is a key pillar of the Government’s policy for international education, as set out in Global Citizens 2030: Ireland’s International Talent and Innovation Strategy to 2030. The TrustEd Ireland Mark will be awarded by QQI to higher education and English language education providers who have demonstrated that they meet new national standards to ensure a quality experience for international learners.

The new TrustEd Ireland scheme will establish, for the first time, a formal quality assurance process for the English language education sector in Ireland and will provide QQI with statutory powers to regulate this sector. QQI's first application cycle for providers seeking to obtain the TrustEd Ireland Mark opened on 14th October 2024 and closed on 28th March 2025. A total of 47 applications (30 higher education providers and 17 English language education providers) were received, and the assessment process is nearing completion. The second application cycle opened on 13th October 2025 and will run until 27th March 2026. A total of 56 providers expressed an interest in applying via the English language education pathway, with 8 providers indicating their intention to apply via the higher education pathway. The second cohort of successful providers will be authorised to use the Mark in 2027.

summary.i: Question No. 1159 answered with Question No. 1158.

question.p: 1161. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the courses in English as a second language currently available for EU and non-EU citizens resident in Ireland; the number of adults who have availed of such courses over the past five years before being granted right to remain; and the number of adults who have availed of such courses over the past five years before achieving Irish citizenship. [71528/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (Deputy James Lawless)
speech.p: In the Further Education and Training (FET) sector, all 16 Education and Training Boards (ETBs) offer free English to Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) classes, as part of their Adult Literacy provision, to meet the day-to-day social, cultural and work-related language needs of new community members. Priority is given to unemployed migrants, International Protection Applicants (IPAs) and refugees with limited or no English language skills. The goal is to help them achieve functional language proficiency, fostering social cohesion and creating pathways to education, training, pre-vocational opportunities, and work.

ESOL provision is available at all levels, from beginner to advanced. Courses be unaccredited or accredited at levels 1 to 6 of the National Framework for Qualifications or through other systems such as Cambridge English Qualifications.
SOLAS has advised my officials that provisional figures from its Programme Learner Support System (PLSS) reports that from January until end of November 2025, ETBs have provided 4,572 ESOL courses.

It is important to note that PLSS does not collect data on the numbers availing of such courses before being granted leave to remain. However, SOLAS has provided provisional PLSS figures relating to the enrolment of IPAs in ESOL since 2022 in the table below.
Comparable data for 2020 and 2021 is not available.
PLSS does not gather data from learners relating to Irish citizenship. However, the following provisional PLSS figures may be of interest to the Deputy.
Comparable data for 2020 is not available. Not all learners provide information about their nationality.

Since the onset of the war in Ukraine in early 2022, the FET sector mobilised rapidly to support Ukrainian refugees, particularly through the significant scaling up of ESOL courses. This impact is clearly demonstrated in the figures presented in the table above.

question.p: 1162. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science for an update on the measures being introduced to improve pay and conditions for teachers of English as a second language to adult immigrants. [71531/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: I would like to take this opportunity to acknowledge the exceptional work carried out by tutors delivering English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) programmes in the Education and Training Boards (ETBs) since 2022 in response to the significant demand arising from the arrival of people displaced by the war in Ukraine. Their efforts have been critical in supporting integration and access to education for those affected.

ETBs employ staff to deliver ESOL programmes under the terms and conditions of tutors or the new Adult Educator grade. It is important to note that there is no separate grade of “teacher of English” within the Further Education and Training sector.Substantial work has been undertaken over a number of years by my Department, the Department of Education and Youth, the Department of Public Expenditure, Education and Training Boards Ireland, SIPTU and TUI to improve pay and conditions for these tutors. In March 2024, agreement was reached between all parties to establish a new Adult Educator grade. This grade provides a standardised pay scale aligned to the Youthreach Resource Person grade, offering incremental progression, including those delivering ESOL programmes. Existing tutors may opt to convert to the new grade or remain on the hourly tutor rate.
ETBs are currently overseeing the implementation process for the new grade. My Department is continuing to monitor progress to ensure full implementation of these measures.

question.p: 1163. Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to introduce legislation establishing a permanent cohort of English as a second language teachers in order to better provide for the needs of adult immigrants lacking a fluency in English; and to ensure that such teachers are given a contract that allows for teaching to be done in the evening, as well as during the day and during the summer holidays (details supplied). [71534/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (Deputy James Lawless)
speech.p: I would like to take this opportunity to acknowledge the exceptional work carried out by tutors delivering English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) programmes in the Education and Training Boards (ETBs) since 2022 in response to the significant demand arising from the arrival of people displaced by the war in Ukraine. Their efforts have been critical in supporting integration and access to education for those affected.

It is my view that legislation is not required to create teachers for a specific subject within the Further Education and Training (FET) sector. ESOL provision is already delivered by staff employed under existing grades and terms, including tutors and the newly established Adult Educator grade which enables the service to be delivered in accordance with the needs of the learners, including summer and evening provision. This ensures an agile FET system with an ability to be responsive to dynamic local education, training and community needs. Such staff, and their contracts and hours, are managed within the parameters of employment law including the Fixed Term Workers Act 2003.
It should also be noted that individual ETBs are the employers and, as such, are responsible for staffing matters with Ministerial consents and approvals as may be determined from time to time.

question.p: 1166. Deputy Natasha Newsome Drennan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the status of the removal of the colour vision test for apprentice plumbers; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71647/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: Currently, 14 apprenticeship programmes require candidates to pass the Ishihara colour vision test, a standard diagnostic test for colour vision deficiency (CVD), before starting training. This has been the case throughout the lifetime of the standards-based apprenticeship approach, which was introduced in the 1990s. There is currently no exemption from this requirement, as all apprenticeships are national programmes, delivered and administered to a common national standard.
The following are the affected apprenticeship programmes:
• Painting and Decorating
• Plumbing
• Mechanical Automation and Maintenance Fitting
• Aircraft Mechanic
• Electrical
• Electrical Instrumentation
• Electronic Security Systems
• Instrumentation
• Refrigeration and Air Conditioning
• Agricultural Mechanics
• Motor Mechanics
• Construction Plant Fitting
• Heavy Vehicle Mechanics
• Vehicle Body Repairs.

SOLAS commissioned an independent report to consider this issue, which has now been completed. Following consideration of this report and its recommendations, SOLAS has advised my Department that it will revise the requirements for colour vision testing in early 2026, and that details of this change will be communicated clearly to employers and other key stakeholders before the end of the year.

question.p: 1167. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the WTE staff, by job title currently working in the National Apprenticeship Office. [71704/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: SOLAS is the State agency with responsibility for further education and training. The Department sets the overall staffing numbers for SOLAS, which includes the National Apprenticeship Office. It is then the responsibility of SOLAS to manage and allocate these resources effectively.
The approved staffing numbers for SOLAS in 2026 is 276 Full Time Equivalent (FTE), an increase from 261 FTE in 2025.

question.p: 1168. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if he will reconsider and reintroduce the 33% reduction on contributory fees for apprentices which was reduced to 17% in the recent budget; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71831/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: I am conscious of financial challenges facing learners and the need for the progressive implementation of measures to address costs as a barrier to attending tertiary education. It is a priority for me to explore the most effective and sustainable ways to support learners in managing these costs.

As part of Budget 2026, I announced a permanent reduction in the Student Contribution charge. This flat rate reduction has reduced the rate from €3,000 to €2,500 for undergraduate students eligible for the free fees initiative and, applied on a pro rata basis, has lowered the student contribution by 17% for apprentices attending Higher Education. This will benefit approximately 14,000 apprentices in the 2025/26 academic year.

As part of Budget 2026, it was important for me to make permanent, sustainable interventions which would give families and learners certainty. With this permanent measure I have done that. This is the first time the student contribution has been permanently reduced.
Looking ahead to future Budget decisions, I will continue to consider all options available to me to reduce the cost of education for apprentices, students and their families.

question.p: 1169. Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plans to expand mental health supports in the further education and training sector. [71832/25]

1170. Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the mental health supports in the further education and training sector available to students. [71833/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1169 and 1170 together.
I welcome the Deputy’s concern for the mental health and well-being of students in the Further Education and Training (FET) sector.

The “Framework for Further Education and Training: Mental Health and Wellbeing” is a key resource for mental health currently in use by Education and Training Boards (ETBs) for the FET sector. Education and Training Boards Ireland (ETBI) developed the Framework in 2023. Its purpose is to provide clear guidance on how ETBs can support learners’ overall well-being and respond to mental health and wellbeing critical incidents in a consistent, planned, and structured manner.

Building on this Framework, ETBI also offers the FET Learner Mental Health & Wellbeing Accreditation Programme. This recognises the work of staff and learners and celebrates initiatives that promote positive mental health and wellbeing within FET. It aims to promote good practice. ETBI launched the fourth iteration, for the 2025/2026 academic year, on World Mental Health Day on 10th October.

Several ETBs have implemented additional supports. For example, City of Dublin ETB and Dublin and Dún Laoghaire ETB provide psychological services for FET learners. Whilst Cavan and Monaghan ETB has established a Learner Support Working Group and appointed a Wellbeing Champion. In addition, many Youthreach centres offer needs-based counselling service.

The Fund for Students with Disabilities (FSD) also plays a vital role by providing funding to ETBs to deliver supports that enable students to participate on an equal basis to the peers in Post Leaving Certificate (PLC) courses. Learners with mental health conditions are identified as a priority group in SOLAS’ guidelines for the FSD. SOLAS has advised my officials that over €5 million was allocated for the FSD in 2025. Furthermore, in Budget 2026, I am pleased to report that I secured an additional €2 million for the Fund.

question.p: 1171. Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the grants available to a person (details supplied) enrolled in a course SUSI does not cover; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71992/25]

speech.from: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science
speech.p: As the Minister is aware, the decision on eligibility for a student grant is a matter, in the first instance, for the awarding authority, SUSI to determine. Up until the 2024/25 academic year, there was no fee support for students undertaking part-time courses. In recognition of the importance of flexible learning pathways, the Department introduced a new Part-Time Fee Scheme for Specified Undergraduate Courses in 2024. This scheme provides fee support to eligible part-time students enrolled in specified publicly funded undergraduate courses leading to a major award. It applies to both in-person and blended/hybrid courses and is designed to enhance access to higher education for students from socio-economically disadvantaged backgrounds.

At present, the scheme is limited to undergraduate courses, as the Student Support Act 2011 only permits approval of part-time courses at undergraduate level. The Student Part-Time Fee Scheme Regulations 2025, published on www.irishstatutuebook.ie, outlines the approved courses. I can confirm that the course the student is attending is not on the approved list. The Department is committed to supporting flexible forms of learning and will keep the policies surrounding support for part-time students under review. However, any future expansion of the parameters of the scheme can only be considered in the context of the budgetary allocation, having regard to overall resource constraints and other competing demands in the further and higher education sector.

Students on part-time undergraduate programmes may also be eligible to apply to the Student Assistance Fund (SAF) for financial support. This Fund provides financial support to full and part-time students who are experiencing financial difficulties while attending college and can provide assistance towards their rent, childcare costs, transport costs and books/class materials. I understand that the student to whom the Minister refers has already received financial support through the SAF. In addition, tax relief at the standard rate of tax may also be available in respect of tuition fees paid for approved courses at approved colleges of higher education. Further information on this tax relief is available from the Revenue Commissioners website, www.revenue.ie.

question.p: 1174. Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the number of apprentices, by phase, in Cork, in tabular form. [72121/25]

speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1174 and 1175 together.

Apprentices are employees and are registered by their employers in the Education and Training Board (ETB) region in which the employer is located. This means the apprentice may not necessarily reside in or be originally from that region, and an apprentice who does live in that region could be registered at another ETB.

The below table shows the number of craft apprentices, by phase, currently registered via Cork Education and Training Board (CETB) to complete an apprenticeship. Apprenticeships are national programmes. Apprentices registered at CETB may conduct their ‘off-the-job training’ at national centres outside of this region based on their apprenticeship, availability of courses and position on the national waiting list, where applicable. It should be noted that this data is as per 11 December 2025.

speech.p: SOLAS, the state agency responsible for further and higher education, has advised that data cannot be provided detailing completion times for apprentices in Cork specifically. The current median time to completion across the craft apprenticeship system is 227 weeks. The mandatory time for craft apprenticeship certification is a minimum of 208 weeks and process times for validation of craft certification can take up to 12 weeks.

question.p: 1177. Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht his Department's strategy to expand connected hubs and remote working infrastructure including the potential for new hubs in Clare; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71407/25]

speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: Our Rural Future, the Government's Rural Development Policy, recognises the opportunity for rural rejuvenation that remote working presents and commits to establishing a comprehensive and integrated national network of 400 remote working hubs by the end of 2025. I was delighted to announce at the National Hub Summit recently that we have reached that key target. As of the 8th of December, there are 401 hubs on-boarded to the Connected Hubs platform. In County Clare there are 14 hubs on-boarded, increasing from 10 when the platform was launched in 2021.

My Department has also funded the Broadband Connection Points (BCP) initiative which provides free high-speed broadband WiFi access at 300 locations around the country. Over 60 of these BCPs have established remote working facilities and are on-boarded to the Connected Hubs platform. Details of all the on-boarded hubs are available at www.connectedhubs.ie.

My Department has invested significantly in the establishment and development of remote working hubs through the range of schemes which make up my Department's Rural Development Investment Programme. This includes funding for the development of hubs under schemes such as the Town and Village Renewal Scheme, the Rural Regeneration and Development Fund and LEADER. It is envisaged that this capital funding will continue as part of these schemes with a continued strategic focus for this investment.

In 2021 and 2022, a new targeted scheme was implemented to support the development of facilities in hubs across Ireland including additional desk space, privacy booths, technical equipment, meeting facilities and access control. Almost €14 million in funding to some 200 projects was allocated via the 'Connected Hub Calls'.

I intend to publish a first National Hubs Strategy shortly, developed jointly with the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment and the Western Development Commission and following consultation with key stakeholders. The strategy will present a coherent approach to the future development of remote working hubs and will include measures to underpin the sustainable development of the Connected Hubs network as well as supporting balanced regional economic development and digital services for rural communities.

question.p: 1178. Deputy Michael Murphy asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if his Department's Community Centres Investment Fund can provide support in circumstances where an existing community centre, due to age, structural condition or non-compliance with modern standards, must be demolished and fully rebuilt; if such full-rebuild projects are eligible for funding under any strand of the scheme; if not, whether the eligibility can be changed for 2026; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [71548/25]

speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: The Community Centre Investment Fund (CCIF) was introduced to provide high quality, accessible, community spaces that are available to all groups in all communities in both rural and urban areas. Some €110 million has been allocated since 2022 for the enhancement and refurbishment of existing community centres and the construction of new centres.

I am committed to delivering further iterations of the scheme in the coming years in line with the commitment in the Programme for Government for this to become a permanent rolling fund. I expect to announce the next round of CCIF early next year, which will focus on refurbishment work in existing community centres. The details in this regard are currently being finalised.

My Department also supports community facilities with enhancement works through a range of other funding streams including through the CLÁR programme, LEADER and the Town and Village Renewal Scheme. I would encourage any interested organisations to check my Department’s website for information on funding opportunities and announcements.

question.p: 1182. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the bilateral meetings he has had with his EU counterparts to date in 2025, in tabular form. [71703/25]

speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: As Minister my main formal interactions at European Union level relate to my role as Minister for Social Protection. Last month, I utilised the plenary session of the European Parliament in Strasbourg to discuss and raise awareness of the issues relating to both Ministerial briefs, in the context of Irelands upcoming Presidency of the European Union.

While in Strasbourg I had a series of high-level discussions with the European Parliament’s Employment and Social Affairs Committee (EMPL). At these meetings I had the opportunity to highlight Ireland's focus on reducing poverty and ensuring equal opportunities. I also had the opportunity to meet with Rafael Benitez, Director of the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe, EMPL Chair Li Andersson and senior members of the European Parliament, including Irish MEPs. I reiterated Ireland’s view that the Council of Europe remains a key European institution safeguarding human rights, democracy and the rule of law. These meetings were primarily related to my social protection brief, but with strong links to the community development and social inclusion elements of the work of the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht.

I also met with a number of Irish MEPs to discuss LEADER funding in the context of the next Multiannual Financial Framework and advocating for a well funded CAP that supports farm resilience, environmental ambition, and rural development measures such as LEADER. In this context I would note that the Department of Agriculture Food and the Marine has established a CAP Consultative Committee, to facilitate the current negotiation process for the post 2027 period, and this committee includes representation from my Department.

While in Strasbourg I also met the EP Intergroup on Traditional Minorities, National Communities and Languages. I engaged with the group’s members on a range of issues including reinforcing the role of Irish as the community language of the Gaeltacht as well as its promotion at national level and efforts to enhance the use of Irish in public services in Ireland. On this issue, in October, I met with a delegation from the Finnish Parliament to discuss how the Irish language is promoted in the Gaeltacht. The delegation included; Dr Jussi Halla-aho, Speaker of Eduskunta, the Parliament of Finland, Mr Mikko Savola, MP and Ms Jenna Simula, MP.

I am hopeful that this engagement with by EU colleagues will help develop a focus on issues relating to the work of my Department, and contribute to a successful Presidency of the EU in the latter half of 2026.

question.p: 1183. Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if he plans to have a children's Irish-language publishing fund or a young writers Irish initiative for young Gaeilgeoirí. [71774/25]

speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: I understaand that Foras na Gaeilge has delivered initiatives to support the publication of works in Irish by young writers over the past number of years and will continue to build on these areas in 2026. These include:
• Scríobh Leabhar (www.forasnagaeilge.ie/scriobhleabhar/) 2025-2026: The aim of this initiative is to give an opportunity to children to write, design and publish their own books in Irish.

• Mentoring Scheme: Clár na Leabhar Gaeilge hopes to advertise this scheme in 2026 which gives trainee writers an opportunity to get advice regarding their writing and the art of writing in general from recognised writers.

In addition, under my Department's Scéimeanna Tacaíochta Gaeilge, funds are available to organisations supporting young writers and children’s Irish-language publishing. In this context, Fighting Words na Gaeilge, runs a significant Irish language writing and publishing programme with funding support from my Department. My department has recently awarded €300,000 over a 3-year period (2025-2028, €100,000 in 2025-2026, €100,000 in 2026-2027, €100,000 in 2027-2028) for this scheme.

Fighting Words na Gaeilge works with schools and youth groups in Gaeltacht regions and with Gaelscoileanna across the country. Under this initiative, creative writing workshops, summer camps, clubs and projects are provided free of charge for young writers. Over the past three years, 12 collections of stories in the Scaip an Scéal series were written by children attending Gaeltacht schools from Kerry to Donegal and have been published in print and online by Fighting Words. Most recently - 'Is Fiú an Tairbhe an Trioblóid' was published with eight schools in Gaoth Dobhair in the Donegal Gaeltacht area. In addition to this, '1, 2, Spraoi' is a celebrated project where children write maths stories in Irish, whereby mathematical concepts are communicated and explained for children in story form. Two volumes have been published - in 2024 and 2025 - and again, these publications are available in print and online.

question.p: 1188. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if his Department has received and assessed the application for the refurbishment of a community centre and library (details supplied) in the north-east ward of Cork city; the current status of the proposal within his Department’s capital approvals process; whether any further information has been requested from Cork City Council; and the expected timeline for a final decision on funding, given that Cork City Council has already completed the preparatory work requested by his Department. [72317/25]

speech.from: Minister of State at the Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: The provision of library services is primarily a matter for local authorities in their capacity as library authorities, under the Local Government Act 2001. Accordingly, the upgrade to the Frank O’Connor Library, Mayfield, Cork City, is a matter for Cork City Council in the first instance.The proposal in respect of the library element of the project is currently being progressed through my Department’s Four Stage Capital Management Process, and I can confirm that Stage 2 (Pre -statutory) Approval issued on 27 October 2022. This stage of the review process ensures that the library proposal complies with the requirements of my Department's Public Library National Standards and Benchmarks, which guide the development of the public library service, and it is not linked to any funding stream. The Libraries Capital Programme 2023-2027 is currently fully committed.I am advised by Cork City Council that the extension and refurbishment of the Frank O’Connor Library, Mayfield, incorporating St Joseph’s Community Centre, is categorised as a priority project in the Council’s Development Plan 2022-2028. I am further informed that the Part 8 planning application, as per the Planning and Development Act 2000 (as amended) requirements, was approved by Councillors in October 2024, allowing the proposal to be progressed through the standard planning approval process. The Part 8 approval is the next step in the process of providing a modern multi use facility and places the Mayfield development in a key place for funding applications once the opportunity arises.

question.p: 1189. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht his plans to introduce AI technologies in rural areas; and the way this will be done (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72347/25]

1190. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht there are any opportunities for AI training and the creation of AI-related jobs in rural areas (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [72348/25]

speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: I propose to take Questions Nos. 1189 and 1190 together.

The Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment has overall responsibility with regard to Government strategy on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and that Department launched Ireland’s first National AI Strategy ‘AI – Here for Good’ in July 2021. That strategy was refreshed in November 2024, with the refresh including a focus on raising awareness within small and medium enterprises of the potential benefits of AI, and the role of research institutes in enhancing skills and research outputs in the area. Overall, the National AI Strategy serves as a roadmap for how Ireland can leverage the potential of AI for unlocking productivity, for addressing societal challenges, and for delivering public services. The actions within that strategy are equally applicable for rural enterprises and indeed the strategy specifically notes that investment in AI will be promoted through initiatives with a regional focus, including the Smart Regional Enterprise Innovation Scheme. I would also note that one of the most important drivers of AI usage will be access to appropriate connectivity and, as the Deputy may be aware, the Minister for Culture, Communications, and Sport recently announced that the National Broadband Plan is ahead of its targets, with 440,000 rural households and farms now passed by the network. In addition, investment by my Department in broadband connection points and in the national hub network has opened up opportunities right across rural Ireland. Government supported AI training is also available to all enterprises through entities such as CeADAR (Ireland’s National AI Hub) and Springboard provides a number of training opportunities, in particular through the Technological Universities (springboardcourses.ie/). Skillnet Ireland, an agency of Department of Further and Higher Education, is also helping businesses to address skills needs in AI and provides online Masters programmes in AI (ictskillnet.ie/course-category/artificial-intelligence/). This strategic investment in connectivity and training by the Government will ensure rural areas can yield the same benefits from AI as any other location in the country. My Department is currently developing a successor to Our Rural Future, the whole-of-government policy for rural Ireland for the period 2021-2025. Submissions to the final period of public consultation closed on Friday 12th December, and will be reviewed to inform the new policy. The policy will include a focus on enterprise development, and the emerging opportunities for enterprise development in rural areas.

summary.i: Question No. 1190 answered with Question No. 1189.

question.p: 1191. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht to consider using GAA club facilities in rural areas for additional social enterprises and tourism projects to strengthen local rural communities (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. speech.from: Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht
speech.p: The Government’s Our Rural Future policy contains a wide range of measures aimed at ensuring that all rural areas are attractive places for people to study, live, work and raise their families. Within my own Department, there has been significant funding increases in recent years across the range of capital investment schemes including those referenced by the Deputy such as the CLÁR programme, the Community Centre Investment Fund and the Community Recognition Fund. These have all supported GAA clubs across the county with funding for the provision of enhanced accessibility and improved facilities.

The Programme for Government includes a commitment to publish and implement a new Our Rural Future policy from 2026 and the process of developing this strategy is well underway. My Department is undertaking an extensive programme of consultations which will help shape the new policy. Indeed I have recently met with the GAA to discuss issues related to rural development and our shared ambitions for rural Ireland. While the facilities and initiatives available through GAA clubs vary across the county and are a matter for the county boards and local clubs, together with my Government colleagues, we will continue to support the improvement of such facilities to build resilience and capacity within rural areas.
